"""What it costs to take the look from a standstill, and what a wind-up buys back. The scripted recipe flicks while already reversing, which is efficient but sloppy: the entry speed is whatever the approach happened to leave, so the same flick lands at a different place every time. The obvious alternative is to stop, settle upright, and then look once - except that a one-sided flick is a forward acceleration, and with no reverse momentum to cancel it the robot keeps the speed it gains. This measures three entries over randomised robots, from the moment the robot is settled and still: plain settled at 0 deg, then flick (what "stop, then look once" costs) wind-up settled, reverse command for W s, then flick (a short local run-up, still from a stop) pullback the above, plus a reverse command held through the recovery What matters is `forward` - how far past the settled standoff the robot ever gets - because that is what eats the margin to the drop, and `peak`, because the angle is what decides whether it sees anything at all. python sim/stairs_windup.py # the full table python sim/stairs_windup.py --trials 8 """ import argparse, math, pathlib, sys import numpy as np HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE)) sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE.parent / "ml")) from botsim import BotSim, LIB, CTRL_DT # noqa: E402 from stairs_probe import model_xml # noqa: E402 SETTLE_MAX = 3.0 # s to wait for "settled": it always takes well under this def settle(sim): """Stand still at 0 deg: the state the look is supposed to start from.""" sim.cmd.v = 0.0 for _ in range(int(SETTLE_MAX / CTRL_DT)): o = sim.step() if o.state != 4: return None if abs(o.pitch) < 0.01 and abs(o.pitch_rate) < 0.20 and abs(o.v) < 0.02: return o return o def episode(tgt, wind, pullback, seed, gain=0.5): """One look from a standstill. Returns (peak deg, forward mm, back mm, upright).""" sim = BotSim(xml_str=model_xml(0.10, 0.30, 6, edge=4.0), seed=seed, randomize=True) sim.place(pitch=0.0, x=2.2) sim.hold(0.6) sim.cmd.mode = 0 if settle(sim) is None: sim.close() return None x_stand = float(sim.d.qpos[0]) # the standoff the look is taken from if wind > 0: sim.cmd.v = -0.35 for _ in range(int(wind / CTRL_DT)): if sim.step().state != 4: sim.close() return None LIB.bot_look_gains(sim.ctl, 4.0, 2.0, gain) LIB.bot_look(sim.ctl, 1, tgt, 0.0) sim.cmd.v = -0.5 if pullback else 0.0 v_entry = float(sim.out.v) # the speed the flick is actually entered at peak, x_far, x_near, bad = 0.0, x_stand, x_stand, False for k in range(int(3.0 / CTRL_DT)): o = sim.step() if o.state != 4: bad = True break peak = max(peak, float(o.pitch)) x = float(sim.d.qpos[0]) x_far, x_near = max(x_far, x), min(x_near, x) if pullback and k > int(1.6 / CTRL_DT): sim.cmd.v = 0.0 # stop pulling back once the nod is over sim.close() return (math.degrees(peak), (x_far - x_stand) * 1000, (x_stand - x_near) * 1000, 0.0 if bad else 1.0, v_entry) def table(trials): print(f"\n\033[1mThe look taken from a standstill: {trials} randomised robots each\033[0m") print(" 'forward' is how far past the settled standoff it ever gets - the margin it spends.") print(f"\n {'entry':<22} {'target':>7} {'v at flick':>11} {'peak':>10} {'forward':>14} " f"{'back first':>12} {'upright':>8}") rows = [] for name, wind, pull in (("stop, then flick", 0.0, False), ("stop, wind 0.35 s", 0.35, False), ("stop, wind 0.60 s", 0.60, False), ("stop, wind 0.90 s", 0.90, False), ("stop, wind 0.90 s + pull", 0.90, True)): for tgt in (0.75, 0.90, 1.00): out = [episode(tgt, wind, pull, 700 + k) for k in range(trials)] a = np.array([o for o in out if o is not None]) if not len(a): print(f" {name:<22} {tgt:7.2f} lost every robot") continue print(f" {name:<22} {tgt:7.2f} {a[:, 4].mean():+8.2f} m/s {a[:, 0].mean():5.1f}+-{a[:, 0].std():2.0f}d " f"{a[:, 1].mean():+8.0f}+-{a[:, 1].std():3.0f} mm {a[:, 2].mean():9.0f} mm " f"{a[:, 3].mean():7.0%}") rows.append((name, tgt, a[:, 0].mean(), a[:, 1].mean(), a[:, 2].mean(), a[:, 3].mean())) return rows def main(): ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--trials", type=int, default=6) a = ap.parse_args() rows = table(a.trials) best = min((r for r in rows if r[2] > 30 and r[5] == 1.0), key=lambda r: r[3], default=None) if best: print(f"\n cheapest entry that still reaches 30 deg on every robot: {best[0]} at {best[1]:.2f} rad, " f"{best[3]:+.0f} mm forward") if __name__ == "__main__": main()

"""A VL53L5CX as the robot would actually have it: 8 x 8 zones, 45 x 45 degrees, bearing resolved. Why this sensor changes the problem. Every number in the stair work so far is limited by one thing: a ray can only reach the first tread if it clears the step nose AND lands before the next one, which needs tan(a) between (h + rise)/(D + tread) and h/D. Those are compatible only when D < h * tread / rise and the landing occludes everything below it short of the edge, so the vertical riser face is never visible from behind the edge at any angle. The limit is the sensor HEIGHT, and it is why a 170 mm riser is unreachable beyond 408 mm even from the lidar at 231 mm - and why mounting a time-of-flight sensor low, as I first suggested, would have been the worst possible place for it: at 80 mm the same riser is only reachable inside 141 mm, which is past the point of no return. What the VL53L5CX adds is not reach, it is SIMULTANEITY. The lidar has one scan plane, so it has to pitch the whole robot to put that plane inside the band - which costs travel towards the drop, needs a wind-up, and is why the recipe takes three looks to answer a third of the time. A 45 degree vertical field of view spans every angle in the band at once, from a standstill, with no nod at all. python sim/tof_sensor.py --band # zones on the tread, by tilt and standoff python sim/tof_sensor.py --tilt 33 # one tilt, per-riser """ import argparse, math, pathlib, sys import numpy as np HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE)) sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE.parent / "ml")) from botsim import BotSim, CTRL_DT # noqa: E402 from stairs_probe import model_xml # noqa: E402 N = 8 # 8 x 8 zones FOV = math.radians(45.0) # 45 x 45 degrees of detection volume ZONE = FOV / N # 5.625 deg per zone TOF_X = 0.032 # body frame: on the front panel face TOF_Z = 0.140 # body frame -> 194 mm above ground, the top of the front panel TOF_TILT = 30.0 # degrees below horizontal. Measured in --measure: best answer rate # (27/30 at a 250 mm standoff against 26 at 35 deg and 23 at 40) while # still seeing floor 1.47 m ahead, so it can do the sonar's job too R_MIN, R_MAX = 0.02, 4.00 # datasheet range per zone NEAR_MM, NEAR_ERR = 200.0, 0.015 # +-15 mm below 200 mm (2.7 sigma, continuous mode) FAR_ERR = 0.05 # +-5 % beyond, in the dark; 8-11 % in 5 klux ambient EDGE = 1.2 SUB = ((0.0, 0.0), (-0.35, -0.35), (0.35, -0.35), (-0.35, 0.35), (0.35, 0.35)) def zone_dirs(tilt, n=N, fov=FOV, sub=SUB): """Rays per zone, in the body frame, for a sensor pitched `tilt` below +x. A zone is not a ray: it is a 5.6 degree cone, and the part reports the NEAREST target in it. That matters most exactly where this robot looks - a zone straddling the step nose sees landing and tread at once and latches the near one. Modelling a zone as its centre ray alone would quietly remove every mixed pixel from the problem, so each zone gets `sub` rays across its own footprint and the reading is their minimum. """ out = [] for r in range(n): for c in range(n): for (du, dv) in sub: el = tilt + (r - (n - 1) / 2 + dv) * (fov / n) az = (c - (n - 1) / 2 + du) * (fov / n) v = np.array([math.cos(el) * math.cos(az), math.cos(el) * math.sin(az), -math.sin(el)]) out.append(v / np.linalg.norm(v)) return out def xml_with_tof(tilt, rise, tread, steps=6, edge=EDGE, height=TOF_Z, base=None): """The stairs model with 64 rangefinders standing in for the zone array.""" xml = base if base is not None else model_xml(rise, tread, steps, edge) dirs = zone_dirs(tilt) sites = "".join(f'<site name="tof{i}" pos="{TOF_X} 0 {height}" ' f'zaxis="{d[0]:.6f} {d[1]:.6f} {d[2]:.6f}" size="0.002"/>' for i, d in enumerate(dirs)) sens = "".join(f'<rangefinder name="tof{i}" site="tof{i}" cutoff="{R_MAX}"/>' for i in range(len(dirs))) old_site = '<site name="sonar" pos="0.032 0 0.080" zaxis="1 0 0" size="0.003"/>' old_sens = '<rangefinder name="sonar" site="sonar" cutoff="4"/>' assert old_site in xml and old_sens in xml, "the sonar site moved: update this script" return xml.replace(old_site, sites).replace(old_sens, sens), len(dirs) class Tof: """Reads the array and turns it into what the sensor actually hands over: a cloud with bearings. The per-zone range noise follows the datasheet - +-15 mm below 200 mm, +-5 % beyond, both 2.7 sigma in the dark - and zones with no return inside 4 m are dropped rather than reported as 4 m, which is what target status does on the real part. """ def __init__(self, sim, n_rays, rng=None, sub=len(SUB), tilt=math.radians(TOF_TILT), height=TOF_Z): self.sim, self.n, self.sub = sim, n_rays, sub self.tilt, self.height = tilt, height self.adr = np.array([sim.m.sensor(f"tof{i}").adr[0] for i in range(n_rays)]) self.sid = np.array([sim.m.site(f"tof{i}").id for i in range(n_rays)]) self.rng = rng or np.random.default_rng(0) def frame(self): """The 8 x 8 range image, in metres, NaN where the zone had no valid target. Each zone is the nearest of its sub-rays, which is what the part reports; the noise is applied once per zone, not per ray, because it is one measurement. """ r = np.array(self.sim.d.sensordata[self.adr], dtype=float) r[(r <= R_MIN) | (r >= R_MAX)] = np.nan if self.sub > 1: g = r.reshape(-1, self.sub) any_hit = np.isfinite(g).any(axis=1) # a zone with no sub-ray hit has no target z = np.full(len(g), np.nan) z[any_hit] = np.nanmin(g[any_hit], axis=1) else: z = r sd = np.where(z < NEAR_MM / 1000.0, NEAR_ERR, FAR_ERR * z) / 2.7 z = z + self.rng.normal(0, 1, len(z)) * sd return z.reshape(N, N) def cloud_body(self, frame=None, tilt=None): """The same points in the ROBOT's frame, which is where a yaw error exists at all. In world coordinates the edge is the same straight line however the robot is turned, so a line fit there measures nothing - it took a nonsense calibration table to notice. The array reports ranges along known bearings, so the body frame is the natural one: no pose needed. """ r = (self.frame() if frame is None else frame).reshape(-1) ok = np.isfinite(r) if not ok.any(): return np.zeros((0, 3)) dirs = np.array(zone_dirs(self.tilt if tilt is None else tilt))[::self.sub] org = np.array([TOF_X, 0.0, self.height]) return org + r[ok][:, None] * dirs[ok] def cloud(self, frame=None): """World points, one per valid zone, placed along the zone's CENTRE ray. The bearing is known per zone, which is the whole point: a sonar hands back one number with no direction and cannot measure a height difference. The centre ray is the right direction to use because that is all the real part reports - the range came from somewhere in the cone, and the robot has to assume the middle of it. """ r = (self.frame() if frame is None else frame).reshape(-1) ok = np.isfinite(r) if not ok.any(): return np.zeros((0, 3)) d = self.sim.d centre = self.sid.reshape(-1, self.sub)[:, 0] # sub-ray 0 is the zone centre org = d.site_xpos[centre[ok]] zax = d.site_xmat[centre[ok]].reshape(-1, 3, 3)[:, :, 2] return org + r[ok][:, None] * zax def edge_skew(pts_body, drop_z, tol=0.025, min_side=2): """How square the robot is to the edge: the LEFT-minus-RIGHT difference in how far the floor runs. Not an angle - a null. Fitting a yaw angle to the edge endpoints looked obvious and was brittle: at 6 degrees of skew some columns see straight past the edge and down the stairs, their furthest landing return is not the edge at all, and the fitted angle saturated around 40 degrees with the sign inverted. The difference between the two halves has none of that trouble. It is zero when square, it changes sign with the skew, and turning until it is zero is all the robot needs. Positive means the floor runs further on the LEFT, so the robot should turn left to square up. Returns None when either half cannot see the edge. """ if len(pts_body) < 2 * min_side: return None on = np.abs(pts_body[:, 2] - drop_z) < tol if on.sum() < 2 * min_side: return None q = pts_body[on] # INNER columns only. Using the outer ones looked like more signal and was the problem: at a few # degrees of skew the outermost column has already run past the edge, so its furthest landing # return is bounded by the field of view rather than by the floor, and the difference went # non-monotonic. A narrow pair of windows either side of the centreline stays on the floor. ang = np.degrees(np.arctan2(q[:, 1], q[:, 0])) left = q[(ang > 4.0) & (ang < 16.0)] right = q[(ang < -4.0) & (ang > -16.0)] if len(left) < min_side or len(right) < min_side: return None dl = float(np.sort(left[:, 0])[-min_side:].mean()) dr = float(np.sort(right[:, 0])[-min_side:].mean()) return dict(skew=dl - dr, d_left=dl, d_right=dr) def stand_and_look(tilt, rise, tread, standoff, seed=0, height=TOF_Z, settle=0.8): """Drive nothing: place the robot at a standoff, let it balance, take one frame.""" xml, n = xml_with_tof(tilt, rise, tread, height=height) sim = BotSim(xml_str=xml, seed=seed, randomize=True) sim.place(pitch=0.0, x=EDGE - standoff) sim.hold(0.4) sim.cmd.mode = 0 sim.cmd.v = 0.0 for _ in range(int(settle / CTRL_DT)): if sim.step().state != 4: sim.close() return None, None, None tof = Tof(sim, n, np.random.default_rng(seed)) fr = tof.frame() pts = tof.cloud(fr) landing_z = float(sim.m.geom("landing").pos[2] + sim.m.geom("landing").size[2]) on = ((np.abs(pts[:, 2] - (landing_z - rise)) < 0.02) & (pts[:, 0] > EDGE) & (pts[:, 0] < EDGE + tread)) if len(pts) else np.zeros(0, bool) sim.close() return fr, pts, dict(n_on_tread=int(on.sum()), landing_z=landing_z, n_valid=int(np.isfinite(fr).sum())) def band(tilts, standoffs, rises, tread=0.30, trials=2): print(f"\n\033[1mZones landing on the first tread, 8 x 8 array at {TOF_Z*1000+54.3:.0f} mm above ground" f"\033[0m") print(" one frame, robot standing still, no nod. '--' means the tread was not reachable at all.\n") head = " ".join(f"{r*1000:3.0f}mm" for r in rises) print(f" {'tilt':>5} {'standoff':>9} {head}") for t in tilts: for D in standoffs: cells = [] for rise in rises: got = [] for k in range(trials): _, _, info = stand_and_look(math.radians(t), rise, tread, D, seed=500 + k) got.append(info["n_on_tread"] if info else 0) m = int(np.mean(got)) cells.append(f"{m:5d} " if m else " -- ") print(f" {t:4.0f}d {D*1000:8.0f} mm {' '.join(cells)}") # The reconstruction thresholds are the lidar's: it pours hundreds of returns onto a tread, so it can # demand 80 of them. The array puts 5 to 18 zones there and that is plenty, because every one carries a # bearing. Same rejection rules, counts scaled to the sensor. TOF_MAP = dict(min_pts=3, min_tread_pts=4, min_span=0.020, max_gap=0.300, min_gap=-0.010) def measure(tilt, standoffs, trials=40, seed0=20_000, height=TOF_Z): """One frame, standing still, through the same reconstruction the lidar work uses.""" from stairs_map import reconstruct print(f"\n\033[1mRiser from a single frame, no nod: {trials} randomised staircases per standoff" f"\033[0m") print(f" array {height*1000+54.3:.0f} mm above ground, {math.degrees(tilt):.0f} deg down\n") print(f" {'standoff':>9} {'answered':>10} {'right (<=20mm)':>16} {'riser error':>18}") rows = [] for D in standoffs: errs, ans = [], 0 for k in range(trials): rng = np.random.default_rng(seed0 + k) rise = float(rng.uniform(0.08, 0.17)) tread = float(rng.uniform(0.24, 0.32)) fr, pts, info = stand_and_look(tilt, rise, tread, D, seed=seed0 + k, height=height) if info is None: continue r = reconstruct(pts, info["landing_z"], **TOF_MAP) if r["rise"] is not None: ans += 1 errs.append(abs(r["rise"] - rise) * 1000) e = np.array(errs) ok = int((e <= 20).sum()) if len(e) else 0 rows.append((D, ans, ok, e)) print(f" {D*1000:6.0f} mm {ans:7d}/{trials} {ok:12d}/{trials} " f"{(e.mean() if len(e) else float('nan')):11.1f} +-{(e.std() if len(e) else 0):5.1f} mm") return rows def main(): ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--band", action="store_true") ap.add_argument("--measure", action="store_true") ap.add_argument("--trials", type=int, default=40) ap.add_argument("--tilt", type=float, default=None) a = ap.parse_args() rises = (0.08, 0.10, 0.13, 0.15, 0.17) if a.measure: for t in (20.0, 25.0, 30.0): measure(math.radians(t), (0.25, 0.30, 0.35), trials=a.trials) elif a.band: band((20, 25, 30, 33, 36, 40), (0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40), rises) elif a.tilt is not None: band((a.tilt,), (0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.50), rises, trials=3) else: band((33,), (0.30,), rises) if __name__ == "__main__": main()

import numpy as np, sys, itertools from multiprocessing import Pool from botsim import BotSim, LIB def stand(a): seed,side,ra,hold=a; s=BotSim(seed=seed,randomize=True); LIB.bot_recover(s.ctl,ra,hold); s.place(1.8*side); s.run(2.5) L=np.array(s.log); st=L[:,1].astype(int) first=(np.diff((st==2).astype(int))==1).sum()==1 return bool(L[-1,1]==4 and first) if __name__=="__main__": N=20 with Pool(2) as p: for ra,hold in itertools.product([0.5,1.0,3.0,6.0],[0.0,0.3]): u=p.map(stand,[(7000+i,sd,ra,hold) for i in range(N) for sd in (1,-1)]) print(ra,hold,f"first-try stand-up: {sum(u)}/{2*N}",flush=True)

"""Sweep stand-up parameters over randomised robots, both lying sides (runs in parallel).""" import sys, numpy as np, itertools, math from multiprocessing import Pool from botsim import BotSim, STATES, LIB def trial(args): seed, side, lift, epush, eg, catch, et = args s = BotSim(seed=seed, randomize=True) LIB.bot_tune(s.ctl, lift, 0.6, epush, catch); LIB.bot_lift_mode(s.ctl, 0, eg, et) s.place(pitch=1.8 * side) s.run(5.0) L = np.array(s.log); s.close() st = L[:, 1].astype(int) ok = st[-1] == 4 and np.abs(L[-500:, 2]).max() < math.radians(12) up = np.where(st == 4)[0] return ok, (L[up[0], 0] - 0.3 if len(up) else np.nan), np.abs(L[:, 5]).max(), np.hypot(L[-1, 9], L[-1, 10]) if __name__ == "__main__": N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 6 grid = list(itertools.product([float(v) for v in (sys.argv[2].split(",") if len(sys.argv) > 2 else ["1.6"])], [30], [0.03], [0.35, 0.5], [0, 4, 8])) with Pool(8) as pool: for lift, epush, eg, catch, et in grid: res = pool.map(trial, [(2000 + i, side, lift, epush, eg, catch, et) for i in range(N) for side in (1, -1)]) ok = sum(r[0] for r in res) print(f"lift {lift} epush {epush} eg {eg} catch {catch} et {et}: {ok}/{len(res)} t_up {np.nanmedian([r[1] for r in res]):.2f}s " f"vmax {np.median([r[2] for r in res]):.2f} travel {np.median([r[3] for r in res]):.2f} m", flush=True)

"""Wobble at standstill + push recovery for cheaper motors (MF5015-V2 10T, Damiao DM-H6215) vs the MF6015. Same robot, same firmware controller (libbot.so). Motor = datasheet Kt/back-EMF/resistance/torque cap/mass/inertia. H6215 has a Hall encoder: 14 pole pairs x 6 Hall states = 84 counts/rev (4.3 deg). Two speed models: 'hall-ok' : drive reports a well-filtered speed (1 dps steps, 5 ms lag) -> optimistic 'hall-raw' : speed = count difference over a 20 ms window -> pessimistic""" import math, sys, numpy as np from multiprocessing import Pool import botsim, motor_compare as mc from botsim import BotSim, LIB, Inputs mc.MOTORS["DM-H6215"] = (0.716, 13.3, 2.5, 2.0, 0.360, 600e-7) # Kt from 320 rpm @ 24 V; inertia estimated CASES = [("MF6015-V2 15T (current)", "abs16"), ("MF5015-V2 10T", "abs16"), ("DM-H6215", "hall-ok"), ("DM-H6215", "hall-raw")] class Sim(BotSim): def __init__(self, enc_mode, **kw): super().__init__(**kw); self.enc_mode = enc_mode; self.hist = [] def sense(self): i = super().sense() if self.enc_mode == "abs16": return i s, sd = self.d.sensordata, self.sid q = (s[sd["ql"]], s[sd["qr"]]); step = 2 * math.pi / 84 cq = [math.floor(x / step) * step for x in q] self.hist.append((cq, (s[sd["wl"]], s[sd["wr"]]))) if self.enc_mode == "hall-ok": lag = self.hist[max(0, len(self.hist) - 6)][1] w = [round(math.degrees(x)) * math.pi / 180 for x in lag] else: n = 20; mc.apply_mass(s, name); LIB.bot_torque_limit(s.ctl, tmax) return s def wobble(a): name, enc, seed = a; s = make(name, enc, seed) s.place(0); s.hold(); s.run(2.0); n0 = len(s.log); s.run(10.0) L = np.array(s.log[n0:]); ok = bool((L[:, 1] == 4).all()) pitch = np.degrees(L[:, 2]); x = L[:, 9] - L[0, 9] tq = 0.5 * (L[:, 7] + L[:, 8]); dtq = np.diff(tq) return ok, pitch.std(), np.ptp(pitch), np.ptp(x) * 1000, np.sqrt((dtq ** 2).mean()) def push(a): name, enc, seed, imp = a; IMPS = (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0) with Pool(4) as p: for name, enc in CASES: w = p.map(wobble, [(name, enc, 100 + i) for i in range(N)]) pu = {imp: sum(p.map(push, [(name, enc, 300 + i, imp) for i in range(N)])) for imp in IMPS} d = p.map(drive, [(name, enc, 700 + i) for i in range(N)]) med = lambda k: np.median([x[k] for x in w]) print(f"{name} [{enc}] | standing 10 s: {sum(x[0] for x in w)}/{N} stayed up, pitch rms {med(1):.3f} deg, " f"pitch p-p {med(2):.2f} deg, wheel creep p-p {med(3):.1f} mm, torque jitter {med(4)*1000:.1f} mN·m/step | " f"pushes " + " ".join(f"{k}:{v}/{N}" for k, v in pu.items()) + f" N·s | drive/stop/turn {sum(d)}/{N}", flush=True)

Robot frame: X forward, Y left (wheel axle), Z up, origin on the axle. Ground at z = -WHEEL_R. Layout (bottom to top): - two MF6015 motors back-to-back on a double centre wall, axle at z = 0 - centre gap between the walls: power distribution, regulator, fuse, IMU (right at the axle) - wheel arches over the wheels - battery shelf above the motors, battery strapped on it - upper bay: front panel (LED eyes, camera, sonar), back cover (perfboard + Pi Zero) - lidar on top Parts: body - one print, open front and back. Print standing on its front opening. front - removable front panel, 6 x M3 into heat-set inserts. """Perfboard layout on the 2.54 mm hole grid (component side faces +x, towards the front). Board: standard 5 x 7 cm double-sided FR4, 24 x 18 holes, 70 (robot y) x 50 (robot z), back face at x = X_BACK + BOARD_STANDOFF, centre bc.PB_CENTER. Hole (k, j): y = Y0 + 2.54 k, z = Z0 + 2.54 j (k 0..23, j 0..17). Regions: the ESP32 DevKit sits on two 22-pin female header rows (j 8 and j 17) over y -60..-4; under it there is 8.5 mm of height for flat parts (74AHCT125, resistors). The CAN board stands on spacers at y -64..-31, z 81-91. Plugs go in the free area below the DevKit (y -31..+6, z 77..98). """ import body_case as bc XB = bc.X_BACK + bc.BOARD_STANDOFF # board back face XF = XB + 1.6 # component face CY, CZ = bc.PB_CENTER NK, NJ = 24, 18 # standard 5 x 7 cm board: 24 x 18 holes (432), 2.54 mm, centred Y0 = CY - (NK - 1) * 2.54 / 2 # hole k = 0 at the -Y end (5.8 mm from the edge) Z0 = CZ - (NJ - 1) * 2.54 / 2 # hole j = 0 at the bottom (3.4 mm from the edge) DK_COLS, DK_ROWS = (1, 22), (8, 17) # DevKit female headers: holes k 1-22 on rows j 8 and 17 def hole(k, j): assert 0 <= k < NK and 0 <= j < NJ, (k, j) return (Y0 + 2.54 * k, Z0 + 2.54 * j) # plugs: name -> (k of pin 1, j, pins, pitch in holes, height, kind). Rows j 0 and 3 stay at k >= 12, clear of the # CAN board standing on spacers over k 0-11 (y -64..-31, z 81-91). PLUGS = { "J2": (12, 0, 4, 1, 8.5, "2.54 header + Dupont"), # The zone array is fitted INSTEAD of the sonar, so it takes the sonar's place on the board with # a 6-pin housing: k 12..17 is exactly six holes before J1 at k 18. Only one of J2 / J2T is # populated on a given robot. "J2T": (12, 0, 6, 1, 8.5, "2.54 header + Dupont"), "J1": (18, 0, 2, 2, 8.0, "XT30PW right-angle PCB plug (15 A)"), "J7": (12, 3, 3, 1, 8.5, "2.54 header + Dupont"), "J5": (17, 3, 5, 1, 8.5, "2.54 header + Dupont"), "J3": (1, 6, 4, 1, 8.5, "2.54 header + Dupont"), "J4": (6, 6, 3, 1, 8.5, "2.54 header + Dupont"), "J6": (10, 6, 5, 1, 8.5, "2.54 header + Dupont"), "J8": (16, 6, 6, 1, 8.5, "2.54 header + Dupont"), # IR receivers: 3V3, GND, GPIO13-16 "J9": (22, 6, 1, 1, 8.5, "2.54 header + Dupont"), # power switch OFF: GPIO21 (100 k pull-down on the board) } def plug_pin(name, i): k, j, n, p, h, _ = PLUGS[name] y, z = hole(k + i * p, j) return (XF + h, y, z) # wire end = top of the housing def plug_box(name): k, j, n, p, h, kind = PLUGS[name] y1, z = hole(k, j); y2, _ = hole(k + (n - 1) * p, j) if kind.startswith("XT30"): return (XF, XF + h, (y1 + y2) / 2 - 5.1, (y1 + y2) / 2 + 5.1, z - 2.6, z + 2.6) return (XF, XF + h, y1 - 1.27, y2 + 1.27, z - 2.5, z + 2.5) # flat parts: name -> (k1, j1, k2, j2, height, what). Resistors 1/4 W lying flat, leads 10.16 mm apart (4 holes); # all of them and the 74AHCT125 sit under the DevKit (rows 9-16 are free between its header rows, 8.5 mm of height). PARTS = { "U1 74AHCT125 (DIP-14)": (8, 11, 14, 14, 4.5, "Pi MOSI -> 5 V WS2812 data; 1OE to GND, unused inputs to GND"), "R4 100k (VBAT top)": (1, 10, 5, 10, 2.5, "J7-1 -> GPIO1"), "R5 12k (VBAT bottom)": (1, 11, 5, 11, 2.5, "GPIO1 -> GND"), "R6 100k (dock top)": (1, 12, 5, 12, 2.5, "J7-2 -> GPIO6"), "R7 12k (dock bottom)": (1, 13, 5, 13, 2.5, "GPIO6 -> GND"), "R8 56k (USB top)": (1, 14, 5, 14, 2.5, "J7-3 -> GPIO7"), "R9 10k (USB bottom)": (1, 15, 5, 15, 2.5, "GPIO7 -> GND"), "R2 1k (echo top)": (16, 10, 20, 10, 2.5, "J2-3 -> GPIO11"), "R3 2k (echo bottom)": (16, 11, 20, 11, 2.5, "GPIO11 -> GND"), "R1 330 (eye data)": (16, 12, 20, 12, 2.5, "U1 1Y -> J4-2"), "R10 330 (LED R)": (16, 13, 20, 13, 2.5, "GPIO38 -> J6-2"), "R11 330 (LED G)": (16, 14, 20, 14, 2.5, "GPIO39 -> J6-3"), "R12 330 (LED B)": (16, 15, 20, 15, 2.5, "GPIO40 -> J6-4"), "C1 470 uF 10 V (6.3 x 11)": (22, 0, 23, 0, 11.0, "5 V bus, beside the 5 V input plug J1 (was under J8)"), } def part_box(name): k1, j1, k2, j2, h, _ = PARTS[name] y1, z1 = hole(k1, j1); y2, z2 = hole(k2, j2) if name.startswith("C1"): c = ((y1 + y2) / 2, z1) return (XF, XF + h, c[0] - 3.2, c[0] + 3.2, c[1] - 3.2, c[1] + 3.2) return (XF, XF + h, min(y1, y2) - 1.2, max(y1, y2) + 1.2, min(z1, z2) - 1.2, max(z1, z2) + 1.2)

r[AX[a[-1]]] = -1.0 if a[0] == "-" else 1.0; rows.append(r) det = (rows[0][0] * (rows[1][1] * rows[2][2] - rows[1][2] * rows[2][1]) - rows[0][1] * (rows[1][0] * rows[2][2] - rows[1][2] * rows[2][0]) + rows[0][2] * (rows[1][0] * rows[2][1] - rows[1][1] * rows[2][0])) assert abs(det - 1) < 1e-9, (xr, yr, zr) from OCP.gp import gp_Trsf from OCP.BRepBuilderAPI import BRepBuilderAPI_Transform t = gp_Trsf() t.SetValues(rows[0][0], rows[0][1], rows[0][2], 0, rows[1][0], rows[1][1], rows[1][2], 0, rows[2][0], rows[2][1], rows[2][2], 0) out = cq.Shape.cast(BRepBuilderAPI_Transform(shape.wrapped, t, True).Shape()) return out, (lambda p: tuple(sum(rows[i][j] * p[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3))) PLACE = {} # name -> (axes, ref_model, target): to map model-frame pin positions to the robot frame def to_robot(name, p): axes, ref, tgt = PLACE[name] _, R = orient(cq.Solid.makeBox(1, 1, 1), *axes) a, r = R(p), R(ref) return tuple(tgt[i] + a[i] - r[i] for i in range(3)) def place(shape, axes, ref_model, target, name=None): if name: PLACE[name] = (axes, ref_model, target) s, R = orient(shape, *axes) r = R(ref_model) return s.translate((target[0] - r[0], target[1] - r[1], target[2] - r[2])) def box(x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1): return cq.Solid.makeBox(x1 - x0, y1 - y0, z1 - z0, cq.Vector(x0, y0, z0)) def cyl(p, d, h, axis): # cylinder from point p along +axis return cq.Solid.makeCylinder(d / 2, h, cq.Vector(*p), cq.Vector(*axis)) # ---------------- built from official drawings ---------------- def pi_zero_2w(header=True): """Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, from the official mechanical drawing (RP-008358): 65 x 30 PCB, holes 3.5 in, 58 x 23, 2x20 GPIO header centred 32.5 from the left / 3.5 from the top edge, mini-HDMI at 12.4, micro-USB at 41.4 and 54 on the bottom edge, CSI on the right end. Board frame: x along 65, y along 30 (0 = bottom edge), z up (PCB top = 1.0). Connector heights from their datasheets (mini-HDMI 3.2, micro-USB B 2.6, CSI 1.2 mm, 22-pin FPC).""" pcb = cq.Workplane().add(box(0, 65, 0, 30, 0, 1.0)).edges("|Z").fillet(3.0).val() for (hx, hy) in ((3.5, 3.5), (61.5, 3.5), (61.5, 26.5), (3.5, 26.5)): pcb = pcb.cut(cyl((hx, hy, -1), 2.75, 3, (0, 0, 1))) parts = [pcb, box(12.4 - 5.6, 12.4 + 5.6, -0.5, 7.0, 1.0, 4.2), # mini-HDMI box(41.4 - 4.0, 41.4 + 4.0, -1.0, 4.6, 1.0, 3.6), # micro-USB (OTG data) box(54.0 - 4.0, 54.0 + 4.0, -1.0, 4.6, 1.0, 3.6), # micro-USB (power) box(61.0, 65.5, 7.5, 22.5, 1.0, 2.2), # CSI 22-pin FPC connector box(-1.5, 11.0, 9.5, 21.0, -1.3, 0.0), # microSD socket + card (underside) box(20.0, 34.0, 8.0, 22.0, 1.0, 7.0)] # RP3A0 SiP + small heatsink (14 x 14 x 5) if header: # soldered 2x20 male header: 2.5 mm plastic, pins 6 mm above hx0 = 32.5 - 19 * 2.54 / 2 - 1.27 parts.append(box(hx0, hx0 + 20 * 2.54, 30 - 3.5 - 2.54 / 2 - 1.27, 30 - 3.5 + 2.54 / 2 + 1.27 - 2.54, 1.0, 3.5)) parts.append(box(hx0 + 0.6, hx0 + 20 * 2.54 - 0.6, 30 - 3.5 - 2.54 - 0.6 + 1.27, 30 - 3.5 + 0.6 + 1.27 - 1.27, 3.5, 9.5)) return cq.Compound.makeCompound(parts) def pi_gpio(pin): """Board-frame (x, y) of a GPIO header pin (1..40). Pin 1 is at the left end, inner row (towards the board centre).""" col = (pin - 1) // 2; inner = (pin % 2 == 1) x = 32.5 - 19 * 2.54 / 2 + col * 2.54 y = 30 - 3.5 - (2.54 / 2 if inner else -2.54 / 2) return x, y def esp32_s3_devkitc1(): """ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 v1.1 from Espressif's dimension drawing (DXF/PDF 2022-04-29): 62.74 x 25.4 PCB, 2 x 22 pins 1.27 in from the long edges at 2.54 pitch, the ESP32-S3-WROOM-1 (Espressif STEP) at the top end, two USB-C at the bottom end (UART at 6.0, USB at 19.4 from the left edge). """Parametric MF6015 -> 12 mm hex RC wheel adapter (CadQuery). Print orientation: hex end DOWN on the bed. The 45-degree cone under the flange means no supports are needed, and the motor-facing flange and centering spigot come out as clean top surfaces. Run: python3 wheel_adapter.py -> writes STEP + STL next to this script. """ import cadquery as cq import math, pathlib # ---------------- motor interface (from LKMTECH MF6015 v2 drawing + STEP) ------ BORE_D = 12.7 # motor centering bore, H7 (1/2") SPIGOT_D = 12.6 # printed spigot: tune 12.55-12.70 for a snug slide fit SPIGOT_L = 4.0 # bore is ~17 mm deep, 4 mm is plenty for centering PCD = 25.0 # 4 x M3 bolt circle M3_CLEAR = 3.4 M3_HEAD_CB = 6.0 # counterbore for M3 socket head (5.5 mm head) # ---------------- adapter body ------------------------------------------------- FLANGE_D = 36.0 FLANGE_T = 5.5 # plate under screw heads. M3x8 -> 2.5 mm into motor NECK_D = 18.0 NECK_L = 6.0 # standoff so the wheel clears the motor - set per wheel HEX_AF = 11.95 # 12 mm hex across flats, minus a print tolerance HEX_L = 7.0 # match the depth of your wheel's hex pocket (it must bottom out) M4_INSERT_D = 5.6 # hole for M4 heat-set insert (check your insert's spec) M4_INSERT_L = 9.0 CHAMFER = 0.6 BRIDGE_LAYER = 0.2 # layer height used by the two-layer bridge at the screw-head seats CONE_H = (FLANGE_D - NECK_D) / 2 # 45 degrees -> support-free def build(): # z = 0 is the motor mating face; +z goes into the motor, -z toward the wheel. spigot = (cq.Workplane("XY").circle(SPIGOT_D / 2).extrude(SPIGOT_L) .faces(">Z").edges().chamfer(0.8)) flange = cq.Workplane("XY").circle(FLANGE_D / 2).extrude(-FLANGE_T) cone = (cq.Workplane("XY").workplane(offset=-FLANGE_T) .circle(FLANGE_D / 2).workplane(offset=-CONE_H) .circle(NECK_D / 2).loft()) z0 = -FLANGE_T - CONE_H neck = cq.Workplane("XY").workplane(offset=z0).circle(NECK_D / 2).extrude(-NECK_L) z1 = z0 - NECK_L hexp = (cq.Workplane("XY").workplane(offset=z1) .polygon(6, HEX_AF / math.cos(math.radians(30))).extrude(-HEX_L) .faces("<Z").edges().chamfer(CHAMFER)) body = spigot.union(flange).union(cone).union(neck).union(hexp) zb = z1 - HEX_L # M4 heat-set insert from the hex end, with a 45 deg pointed end (prints without a bridge, hex-down) body = body.cut(cq.Workplane("XY").workplane(offset=zb) .circle(M4_INSERT_D / 2).extrude(M4_INSERT_L)) body = body.cut(cq.Solid.makeCone(M4_INSERT_D / 2, 0.01, M4_INSERT_D / 2, cq.Vector(0, 0, zb + M4_INSERT_L), cq.Vector(0, 0, 1))) # 4 x M3 clearance holes + counterbores opening on the wheel side. The head seat is printed with the # two-layer bridge trick (hex-down): layer 1 leaves a slot as wide as the hole, layer 2 a square, then the round # hole: clean bridges, no sacrificial membrane to drill out, no support. pts_a = [(a, PCD / 2 * math.cos(math.radians(a)), PCD / 2 * math.sin(math.radians(a))) for a in (45, 135, 225, 315)] pts = [(x, y) for _, x, y in pts_a] seat = -FLANGE_T body = body.cut(cq.Workplane("XY").workplane(offset=seat + 2 * BRIDGE_LAYER) .pushPoints(pts).circle(M3_CLEAR / 2).extrude(FLANGE_T + 1)) for a, x, y in pts_a: slot = (cq.Workplane("XY").workplane(offset=seat).center(x, y) .rect(M3_HEAD_CB + 0.4, M3_CLEAR).extrude(BRIDGE_LAYER).rotate((x, y, 0), (x, y, 1), a)) sq = (cq.Workplane("XY").workplane(offset=seat + BRIDGE_LAYER).center(x, y) .rect(M3_CLEAR, M3_CLEAR).extrude(BRIDGE_LAYER + 0.01).rotate((x, y, 0), (x, y, 1), a)) body = body.cut(slot.intersect(cq.Workplane("XY").workplane(offset=seat).center(x, y).circle(M3_HEAD_CB / 2).extrude(BRIDGE_LAYER))).cut(sq) body = body.cut(cq.Workplane("XY").workplane(offset=seat) .pushPoints(pts).circle(M3_HEAD_CB / 2).extrude(-(CONE_H + 1))) # outer edge chamfer on the mating flange return body if __name__ == "__main__": out = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent part = build() cq.exporters.export(part, str(out / "mf6015_hex12_adapter.step")) cq.exporters.export(part, str(out / "mf6015_hex12_adapter.stl"), tolerance=0.02, angularTolerance=0.1) bb = part.val().BoundingBox() print("length %.1f mm, volume %.1f cm3, PETG mass ~%.0f g" % (bb.zlen, part.val().Volume() / 1000, part.val().Volume() / 1000 * 1.27))

"""Check every harness bundle and every plug housing against every part. Overlaps within 7 mm of one of the harness's own pins are the connection itself and are ignored.""" import sys, json, math import robot_paths as RP; RP.add_sources() exec(open(RP.source('real_assembly.py')).read().split('if __name__ == "__main__":')[0]) import wiring as W HS = W.harnesses() targets = dict(PRINTED); targets.update({k: v[0] for k, v in ALL.items()}) def bb_apart(a, b): p, q = a.BoundingBox(), b.BoundingBox() return p.xmax < q.xmin or q.xmax < p.xmin or p.ymax < q.ymin or q.ymax < p.ymin or p.zmax < q.zmin or q.zmax < p.zmin for lbl, shp, col in W.connectors(): for n, s in targets.items(): if bb_apart(shp, s): continue try: v = shp.intersect(s).Volume() except Exception: v = 0 if v > 0.5: print("CONNECTOR", lbl[:44], "x", n[:44], round(v, 1)) res = [] for h in HS: t = W.tube(h["pts"], h["dia"]); hits = [] ends = [c["a"] for c in h["conds"]] + [c["b"] for c in h["conds"]] + [h["pts"][0], h["pts"][-1]] for n, s in targets.items(): if bb_apart(t, s): continue try: i = t.intersect(s) except Exception: continue for so in i.Solids(): if so.Volume() < 0.2: continue c = so.Center(); c = (c.x, c.y, c.z) if min(math.dist(c, e) for e in ends) < 7: continue hits.append((n, round(so.Volume(), 1), [round(v, 1) for v in c])) L = [round(W.length(W.conductor_path(h, c))) for c in h["conds"]] res.append(dict(name=h["name"], wires=len(h["conds"]), length_mm=max(L), hits=hits)) print(f"{h['name'][:50]:50s} {max(L):5d} mm {'OK' if not hits else hits}") json.dump(res, open(RP.out('wire_report.json'), 'w'), indent=1)

# 2-wheel-balanced-bot — notes for Claude Code Two-wheel self-balancing robot, version **V1.1** (body "shape C", lidar, voice orders via Claude, vertical charging dock). The owner is a C++ programmer; explain in C++ terms, keep answers short, and say plainly what was verified (sim, build, check) and what wasn't. ## Hardware in one paragraph 2 × LKMTECH MF6015-V2 hub motors (CAN, torque commands, 0xA1 at 1 Mbps) back-to-back on a printed PETG body; ESP32-S3 DevKitC-1 (balance controller, 500 Hz) on a perfboard with an SN65HVD230 CAN board; Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (lidar LD19, docking, voice, Claude API); 6S 1400 mAh LiPo + 6S BMS, Pololu 2813 push-button power switch (ESP32 GPIO21 can switch it off), 30 A fuse; IMU GY-521; 4 × TSOP38238 IR receivers in hoods on top for the dock's beacon. Dock: printed foot + head + mast, ATtiny85 controller that keeps the sprung brass rods dead unless the robot is on them (sense divider, short = latch off). Full list: `bom/build_bom.py` → BOM xlsx. ## Layout | Folder | What | |---|---| | `core/` | The controller (`controller.cpp/.hpp`), LQR gains (`gains.hpp`, from `sim/design_lqr.py`), learned stand-up policy (`standup_policy.hpp`, generated), C API for the sim (`sim_api.cpp`). The **same C++** runs in the sim and on the ESP32. | | `firmware/esp32/` | PlatformIO (`pio run -e esp32s3`), host tests `test_host/run_tests.sh`. `lib/botcore/` is a COPY of `core/` — keep them in sync after editing `core/`. | | `firmware/dock_beacon/` | ATtiny85 dock controller + `test_dock_logic.cpp`. | | `pi/` | Python on the Pi: `robot/brain.py`, `dock.py` (DockPilot), `ld19.py`, `link.py`; tests `python -m pytest -q` in `pi/` (48). | | `sim/` | MuJoCo + `botsim.py` (loads `libbot.so`/`.dylib`). `run_tests.py` (stand-up, balance, pushes, missions), `dock_sim.py` (40-start docking sweep), `nav_sim.py`, `build_model.py` (regenerates the XML from the CAD), `design_lqr.py 0.06 0.6 10` (the weights we use), `rebuild.sh` (all of that in order). | | `ml/` | RL: the stand-up and the stair-measuring nod, see `ml/README.md`. `setup_mac.sh` (venv, `--cad` also installs CadQuery), `run_training.sh` (the stand-up loop). Stairs: `stairs_env.py` (when to nod), `stairs_baseline.py` (the hand-scripted recipe it has to beat), `train_stairs.py`, `evaluate_stairs.py`. | | `elec/` | `netlist.py` + `erc.py` (electrical rules check; `test_erc.py` mutation tests). Current result: CHECK 3, WARN 1, INFO 5 (all known). | | `cad_src/case/` | CadQuery: `body_case.py` (all printed parts, named constants), `wiring.py` (3D harness routes), `real_assembly.py` (fit check), `wire_check.py`, `export_*`, `assemble.py`. `robot_paths.py` says where everything is — import it, never hard-code a path. `cad_src/rebuild.sh` runs the chain in order. | | `cad/` | Exported STL/STEP for printing. | | `site/` | The project website (same as the Claude artifact). Builders: `build_docs.py`, `build_boards.py`, `build_dock_wiring.py`, `tools/site_rebuild.py`. View: `python3 -m http.server -d site 8000`. | | `tools/` | `make_workspace.sh` (see below), `cad_baseline.py` (CAD regression: volume + bbox of 28 parts), `wc_power.py` (quick wire check of chosen harnesses). | ## Build / check commands Prefer the scripts: each one is the documented sequence, in order, and they are what gets maintained. ```bash ./check.sh # everything checkable here (~40 s): firmware host tests, ERC + its 8 # mutation tests, CAN check, the 48 Pi tests, models + 30-robot sim suite. # Takes section names: ./check.sh elec pi. Exits non-zero on failure. core/build_lib.sh # the controller library: libbot.dylib on macOS, libbot.so elsewhere sim/rebuild.sh # models -> LQR gains -> library -> sim suite ml/run_training.sh # the learned stand-up loop end to end (see ml/README.md) cad_src/rebuild.sh # the CAD chain; --fast skips the two slow viewer exports ``` By hand, when you want one step only: ```bash cd sim && python run_tests.py # 30 robots, ~11 s on an M4 Mac; writes results/report.json cd sim && python dock_sim.py # 40 starts (slow) cd firmware/esp32 && pio run -e esp32s3 && test_host/run_tests.sh cd pi && python -m pytest -q cd elec && python erc.py && python test_erc.py && python erc.py # see the trap below ``` `./check.sh` does not mutate the repo: it snapshots the files the checks regenerate, reports whether a fresh run disagrees with what is committed, and restores them. Last-digit differences in `sim/results/report.json` between macOS/clang and Linux/g++ are normal; a changed success count is not. **Paths.** Every script finds its own files through `cad_src/case/robot_paths.py`, so a plain checkout works with no setup. Override any root with `ROBOT_CASE`, `ROBOT_WHEEL_ADAPTER`, `ROBOT_ROOT`, `ROBOT_OUT`, `ROBOT_MODELS`, `ROBOT_MF6015_STEP`. `BOT_WS` is honoured too, for the workspace `tools/make_workspace.sh` builds (optional now, and only its directories that actually exist are used). Never hard-code a path. Vendor STEP models are not in the repo (licences): `models/fetch_models.sh` downloads the nine that are public, and `models/bought/mf6015.step` must be fetched by hand from the LKMTECH / dealer page. Only the fit and wire checks and the "real parts" view need them; `cad_src/rebuild.sh` checks for them up front. CAD change workflow: `python tools/cad_baseline.py /tmp/before.json` → edit → `cad_baseline.py /tmp/after.json` → compare (refactors must change nothing, all 28 parts). Then `cad_src/rebuild.sh`, which runs `dump_wiring.py` → `assemble.py` → `real_assembly.py` (6 known contacts: mics, camera, OTG) → `wire_check.py` (clean except the known Pi OTG/Dupont contacts) → `export_print_data.py` → the viewer exports → ERC. Then the site builders. ## Traps worth knowing - `elec/test_erc.py` calls `erc.main()`, which overwrites `erc_report.json` with the last mutation case. Run `erc.py` again afterwards. `check.sh` already does. - `ml/train.py` always prints that it saved `best.zip`, but only writes it once `EvalCallback` has fired (~100k steps / n_envs). Short runs leave `latest.zip` only; `run_training.sh` falls back to it. - **`best.zip` does not mean best.** `EvalCallback` ranks checkpoints by eval reward, and that signal is far too noisy here to rank anything (sigma ~2.5 on a mean of ~8). One 2 M-step run's `best.zip` was a 100k-step checkpoint scoring 26/60 compiled while the same run's final policy scored 171/180 - and it was exported and reported as the result. `run_training.sh` now exports and scores *every* candidate with `evaluate.py --compiled` and keeps the winner. Never judge a run by `best.zip` alone. - `evaluate.py <model>` (torch, mode 2) and `evaluate.py --compiled` (the C++ policy, mode 1) can disagree wildly, and only `--compiled` is the gate: it is what the robot runs. The two forward passes differ by ~1e-7 from float32 summation order, which a chaotic swing-up amplifies - traced once to an identical `+1.00000` first action and pitch splitting at the 4th decimal eleven ticks later. A policy whose two numbers disagree by more than a robot or two is sitting on a knife edge; `run_training.sh` prints both and says so. - `cad_src/case/wall_check.py` imports `design_variants`, which is not in the repo. Dead script. - `firmware/esp32/lib/botcore/` is a copy of `core/`: run `sync_core.sh` after editing `core/`. It now verifies the copy with `cmp` and exits non-zero on a mismatch - it used to omit `standup_policy.hpp` and still print "updated", so the ESP32 could have been built against the placeholder policy. - `BotSim.step()` returns `BotSim.out` itself, one ctypes struct the C++ refills in place every tick, not a snapshot. Anything about a particular instant must be copied out before stepping the sim on. Reading `o.pitch_rate` after a later loop reported 5.5 rad/s for a handover that happened at 16.9. - **Publishing `site/index.html` as the Artifact page double-wraps it.** The Artifact tool always wraps the page in its own `<!doctype html><html><head>` skeleton, and `site/index.html` is already a complete document (it has to be - `site/` is served directly too). Publishing it as `file_path` nests one document inside the other: two `<html>`, two `<head>`, and the three.js **importmap** ends up inside the body, so `import 'three'` fails and the 3D viewer renders nothing. Strip the outer `<!DOCTYPE>/<html>/<head>/<body>` tags into a throwaway copy and publish that; keep the repo file a valid standalone page. Supporting files passed in `files` (e.g. `standup.html`) are served unwrapped, so those keep their own doctype. - **A manoeuvre tested on one robot tells you nothing.** `sim/stairs_look.py` ran the look-down nod on a single robot and it worked; over randomised robots it lost 7 in 10, and every failure was a robot that drew two control periods of CAN latency (`BotSim.delay == 2`, which the randomisation draws half the time). At the full LQR pitch gains the nod's PD is a ~130 rad/s rate loop and 4 ms of latency takes it unstable: the pitch rings, the wheels get pumped to 5 m/s and the 114 rad/s runaway guard cuts the motors. Half gains (`look_gain`, as the dock lean already used) gives 10/10 at the same peak pitch. Any new high-gain pitch loop has to be measured against delay-2 robots, not the nominal one. - **Never hand a manoeuvre back to the balance law with `v_ref_ = 0` while the robot is moving.** A 34 deg nod ends at ~0.55 m/s; zeroing the reference demands all of it back in one tick, `K[3]` saturates the torque, the body over-rotates to -20 deg in 30 ms and the wheels run away. Hand over `v_ref_ = phi_rate_ * R` and let the normal `max_accel` ramp take the speed down. Same shape of bug as the stand-up's fixed-torque kick tripping the runaway guard. - **A one-sided flick from a standstill costs ~1 m of travel towards the drop.** A flick IS a forward acceleration, so with no reverse momentum to cancel it the robot keeps what it gains: 0.75 rad (the ~32 deg that can see a tread) costs **+899 +- 264 mm** from a dead stop. Reversing for 0.9 s first - still from a standstill, still one forward look - reaches -0.47 m/s and the same flick costs **+62 +- 86 mm**, 100% upright. `sim/stairs_windup.py` has the table. Corollary: **retrying deeper is a trap.** 0.90 rad costs +504 mm against 0.75 rad's +62 mm, so a deeper second look spends exactly the margin it is trying to earn. Retry closer at the same depth, never deeper. - **A step down has to be COMMITTED to, not reacted to.** Rolling off a lip at walking pace produces no free fall at all - the wheel stays on the corner the whole way down - so the accelerometer never sees anything and `fall_catch` never fires, while the velocity loop watches its support vanish and drives the wheels to -4.9 m/s. The robot does not need to detect the edge: the array measured it. `step_mode` holds attitude across the lip with the speed loop off, armed 20 mm out, and takes a 100 mm step from 0% to 92%, a 170 mm step from 0% to 75%. Three things about it, each learned the hard way: it must LATCH and clear itself (a version that ran while the command was held re-did its handover every tick, which accidentally disabled the position loop - that was most of why it worked, and releasing the command then dropped 98% to 65%); it must not hand back until the landing transient is over (exit 8 ms after touchdown scores 5%, at 0.35 s it throws the body to 112 deg, past ~0.5 s it is fine); and the speed command must be released the moment the edge is crossed, or the robot carries ~300 mm across a 300 mm tread and off the next edge. - **Skew is the failure the attitude hold cannot save, and the array cannot measure it.** A step taken 10 deg off square scores 10-15% against 65-90% square. But at a 280 mm standoff 5 deg of skew moves the edge distance by about 1 mm - under the range noise - and `d = D/cos(psi)` makes the minimum-distance null quadratically flat, so neither a line fit nor a left-right difference resolves it (both were tried; the line fit saturated at 40 deg with the sign inverted). Squareness is HELD by the yaw controller, not sensed: across four landings the drift stays under 0.3 deg. - **The 3D viewer fails SILENTLY - a blank canvas and nothing in the page to say why.** It was dark for a long time because nothing ran it. Three separate faults, each invisible: three.js loaded from a CDN; then an importmap value of `./vendor/three.module.js`, which resolves against the page's base URL and cannot be known for an artifact; then, once the two libraries were concatenated to remove imports entirely, `Identifier '_ray' has already been declared` - both three.js and OrbitControls declare it at module scope, so OrbitControls has to go in a closure. `tools/artifact_page.py` builds the self-contained copy (no skeleton, no imports) and `tools/check_viewer.mjs` EXECUTES it against a DOM stub; `./check.sh site` runs both. Never publish the viewer without that check passing. - **For the descent reward, refusing has to cost MORE than falling.** This inverts the nod's ordering on purpose: there, going over the edge was catastrophic and declining to look was merely useless, so `FELL < NO_NOD`. Here the robot's whole job is to get down, so standing at the top for ever is total failure while a scruffy step is progress. At `NO_STEP = -12` against `FELL = -20` it learned exactly the wrong lesson - `crossed_rate` 0.01 after 800k steps. - **PPO cannot find the step-down recipe from noise, and a warm start is not optional.** Three decisions have to coincide (roll speed, commit within ~2 cm of the edge, release the speed command); a random policy crosses the edge 20 times out of 20 and lands none, so every early trajectory ends identically and there is no gradient. `ml/warmstart_descend.py` clones the scripted recipe (jittered, successes only) and PPO improves from there. - **The 3D viewer's full part set comes from `export_viewer_real.py`, not `export_viewer_data.py`.** The latter alone gives 63 parts and silently drops the `conn` group and every bought component (c_ESP32, k_LD19 ...); the real one gives 111. Both need `models/bought/mf6015.step`. - **three.js is vendored in `site/vendor/`, not loaded from a CDN.** The importmap points at `./vendor/three.module.js`, so the viewer works in the artifact sandbox and offline. - **Going down a step, the robot's enemy is its own velocity loop, not the drop.** One axle means both wheels leave the ground together, and for ~150 ms the balance law servos against nothing: unloaded wheels run 0.56 -> 5.78 m/s in 50 ms and the reaction throws the body to +-90..110 deg, on steps as small as 40 mm. The accelerometer sees it (|a| ~ 2 m/s^2 in free fall, a ~176 m/s^2 spike on touchdown), so `fall_catch` holds the balance law off and damps the wheels only. Two traps inside that: a 25 ms dwell latches AFTER the runaway (use ~6 ms), and leaving on the landing SPIKE is wrong - a wheel clipping the edge reads 18 m/s^2 for one tick, and exiting on that drove the wheels to -3.8 m/s in mid-air. Leave on sustained support instead. - **With `auto_standup` on, a tumble ends "balancing".** Any descent or push measure that only looks at the end state counts a robot that fell over and picked itself up as a success. Score peak pitch as well: adding `peak < 46 deg` turned a 25% "survival" at 100 mm into 0%. - **The 3D viewer cannot be regenerated without `models/bought/mf6015.step`** (not redistributable; `assemble.py` imports it unconditionally). Any CAD change therefore lands in the repo without the viewer being rebuilt until that file is present. - **Sensor HEIGHT is what decides whether a step can be measured at all.** A ray reaches the first tread only if it clears the nose and lands before the next one, which needs `D < h * tread / rise`; and the landing occludes everything below it short of the edge, so the vertical riser face is never visible from behind the edge at any angle. Hence 170 mm risers are unreachable beyond 408 mm even from the lidar at 231 mm, and a time-of-flight sensor mounted LOW would be the worst possible place for one (at 80 mm the same riser needs to be inside 141 mm). The VL53L5CX therefore goes high on the front panel, 194 mm up, looking 30 deg down. - **A zone is a cone, not a ray.** Modelling each VL53L5CX zone as its centre ray alone quietly deletes every mixed pixel from the problem - and this robot looks straight at a depth discontinuity, where mixed pixels live. With 5 sub-rays per zone and the nearest taken, as the part reports, the riser error went from 3.8 mm to 12.8 mm and the success rate from 1.000 to 0.938. The flattering number was the model, not the sensor. - **`bot::Inputs` and `bot::Command` are mirrored by hand in `sim/botsim.py` as ctypes structs.** Adding a field to either in C++ without adding it there shifts every field after it and the sim reads garbage, silently. Check `ctypes.sizeof` against `sizeof` in C++ after any such change. - **GPIO 33-37 are the octal PSRAM bus on the N8R8 module** and 26-32 the flash: a pin assignment there compiles and then does not boot. `elec/erc.py` checks this, and it is what caught the first VL53L5CX pinout. Free on this build: 2, 41, 42, 47 (and the sonar's 10/11 when it is not fitted). - **The sonar's edge event is only a measurement when the body is level and steady.** "The floor echo is gone" means two different things: the floor really ended (the edge), or the beam is pointing over floor that is still there (the robot leaned back). The second fires during every brake and puts +80 mm of error into the distance - towards the drop. The event counts only on a confirmed-floor to lost transition, held two pings, with |pitch| < 0.05 rad and |pitch rate| < 0.6 rad/s. With that gate the estimate runs +3 to +6 mm all episode; without it, +25 to +144 mm. - **Calibrate the event with the SAME detector you run.** The factor turning the event into a distance is defined against a detection rule; a calibration that used a different rule (or a different ping rate) is meaningless. Two copies of the rule drifted apart once and cost a day. `FloorWatch` in `sim/stairs_sonar.py` is the single definition, used by both the calibration and the environment. - **Grazing beams are hopeless range finders.** The floor range goes as h/sin(tilt+15), so its sensitivity to body pitch is h*cos(a)/sin(a)^2: -1.94 m/rad at 0 deg tilt against -0.46 at 15 deg. Measured end to end, the edge event is +141 +- 87 mm at 0 deg and -4 +- 12 mm at 15 deg. More tilt is better until the event falls inside D_FENCE (250 mm), which rules out 20 deg and makes 15 deg the pick for the as-built 134 mm mounting. - **A retry phase that can only reverse walks the robot away from the edge.** The look is entered reversing, so each one ends ~180 mm further back than it started. A reposition step that only closes in when it is too far - and never comes forward when it is too far back - put the third flick's peak pitch at 1200 mm, where nothing is visible: 0 returns on every retry. Reposition from either side. - **Tilting the sonar down makes an edge detector, not a sensor.** Modelled as a real +-15 deg cone taking the nearest echo (`sim/stairs_sonar.py`, which reproduces h/sin(tilt+15) to 4 mm), a 10 deg tilt loses the floor echo at **263 +- 12 mm** from the drop with no odometry involved - the safety signal the margin failures need. But the same reading swings **245 -> 448 mm over +-7 deg of body pitch**, and a balancing robot sways that much holding station, so the forward obstacle stop has to predict the floor range from the IMU and gate it out or it trips constantly. The sonar can never contribute to the reconstruction: one range, no bearing, over a 30 deg cone. - **A riser is a DIFFERENCE between two surfaces, so returns on the tread measure nothing on their own.** `estimate()` finds the landing first and subtracts the first level surface below it; with no returns on the landing it gives `rise=None` however good the view of the tread is. The swing taken from a short standoff fails exactly this way - one episode put 597 rays on the first tread and produced no riser at all, because every ray had cleared the landing. The flick does not have the problem only because it looks from further back while reversing. `n_seen` alone therefore does not mean a measurement: `land_seen` in the info dict says which of the two failures it was. - **`build_model.py --stairs` landings are finite.** The landing runs from `edge - 3.0` to `edge`, so a script that reverses for a second or two can drive off the BACK of it, and that reads exactly like falling over. Two of the nod-cost measurements were wrong that way before the start was moved forward. - **Two scripts wrote `wiring_data.json` with different fields.** `dump_wiring.py` included `awg` and `slack`; `export_viewer_real.py` did not, and measured `L` without the slack. Whichever ran second won, so after a viewer export `elec/can_ground_check.py` died on `KeyError: 'awg'` - and **`check.sh` scored it a pass**, because the command was `python can_ground_check.py | tail -3` and `bash -c` does not inherit the script's `pipefail`, so the status was tail's. Both now call `wiring.harness_record()`, and every `bash -c` in `check.sh` is `bash -o pipefail -c`. Any new piped check has to be too, or a crash reads as a pass. - **`site/build_docs.py` copies the working tree to build the published software zip**, so anything sitting in the repo goes out with it. It swept in `.venv` (~2.4 GB, minutes of build time) and `models/bought/` - the vendor STEP models, which are **not ours to redistribute**. It now has an explicit skip list; keep licence-encumbered files out of it. - `mujoco` is pinned to `==4.0.0` in `ml/requirements.txt` because the committed `sim/results/report.json` is version-dependent. 4.0 split the distribution (mujoco-core + mujoco-studio) and an in-place upgrade from 3.x can delete files that moved: uninstall first. Verified: 4.0.0 reproduces the committed counts. ## Rules that must not be broken - **No secrets in git.** The Claude API key lives only in `/etc/robot.env` on the Pi (root, chmod 600), loaded by `EnvironmentFile=-/etc/robot.env` in `robot.service`. Never in `config.json`. `.gitignore` blocks `*.env`. - **Dock safety:** the rods are dead unless the robot's detect divider is sensed (ADC 310–480); ON check < 15 V → fault; 3 faults → latched. Don't weaken this. - **Power:** XT60s between the back-cover module and the body are gender-keyed (battery side female in, switch side female out). Peak current on the main feed 18.9 A (ERC). - Keep `firmware/esp32/lib/botcore/` = `core/`. - After any site change: rebuild and commit `site/` (the owner wants the site kept in the repo). ## State (Nov 2026) and open points - Shelf raised 10 mm (SHELF_Z 47, Z_TOP 152) so the motor leads loop gently; back cover unplugs as a module. - Cost: CoM 40.6 mm above the axle → hand-tuned stand-up 25/30 face-down, 23/30 back-down within 5 s (was 30/30), 52/60 within 12 s; docking 34/40 (was 37/40). - **The learned stand-up now beats the hand-tuned one in the sim** (Nov 2026, third training run): `evaluate.py --compiled` 60/60 on the usual seeds 3000-3029 and 60/60 on two held-out sets (9000, 12000), against 155/180 for the hand-tuned one; median travel 0.84 m vs 0.97. It hands over to the balance controller at 1.77 rad/s against the hand-tuned 3.66, and reaches the catch far more repeatably (p90 0.80 s vs 1.64 s). `core/standup_policy.hpp` holds the trained weights and `STANDUP_POLICY_TRAINED` is `true`, **but `standup_mode` is still 0** (`core/controller.hpp:104`), so the robot behaves exactly as before. The sim gate is met; flipping it to 1 is a hardware decision and has not been taken. - **The shipped policy was trained at 1.2 rad, and that is better than training on the real task.** The curriculum ratchet used to gate on full success (~12%), never cleared `UP_OK`, and left every worker at `PITCH_START` for all 2 M steps - it had silently collapsed to "always train at 1.2 rad". That gate is now fixed (it ratchets on a catchable handover: a success, or `gentle >= GENTLE_OK`, i.e. pitch rate <= ~6.7 rad/s) and verified: a fourth run climbed to the real 1.8 rad by 200k steps and stayed there. It scored **171/180**, against **180/180** for the policy trained entirely at 1.2 rad. So the easy start pitch is a better teacher, not a lucky accident - the alternative was measured. The shipped weights are therefore the ones from before the gate was fixed: to regenerate them, check out `ml/` at `e4c9d26`. Retraining with today's `ml/` should land near 171/180, which still beats the hand-tuned 155/180. - `env/success_rate` (caught first attempt, survived 1 s) is not the same measure as `evaluate.py` (upright within 5 s, retries allowed), which is why one reads ~0.13 where the other reads 1.00. Still open, and still worth reconciling: the gate is `evaluate.py`. - Earlier runs failed for reward-design reasons, both diagnosed, both worth not repeating: run 1 (`ent_coef` 0) annealed its exploration away before ever reaching the success bonus; run 2 gave a flat +2.0 for touching the catch window, so the policy slammed through it at 16.9 rad/s and lost all 60. The fix was to scale that credit by `exp(-(rate/8)^2)`. `ml/train.py` now logs `env/catch_rate_rad_s`, `env/catch_v_m_s`, `env/success_rate` and `env/start_pitch` to TensorBoard: the eval-reward curve alone (sigma ~2.5) would not have shown either failure, and both were obvious in those four numbers within 100 k steps. - Demo videos in `site/files/` still show the pre-raise body. - `ml/evaluate.py` used to fail on macOS (multiprocessing spawns there, so the workers never saw the model path); fixed. - Motors: cheaper alternatives were reviewed (StepperOnline, PGFUN, VXB, gimbal motors): none fits; the only candidate is a low-KV outrunner + ODESC driver, not pursued.

# Testing the CAN driver and code Three levels, cheapest first. Do them in order: each one rules out a class of problems before the next. ## 1. Unit tests on the PC (no hardware) ``` firmware/esp32/test_host/run_tests.sh ``` Builds `src/lk_motor.cpp` unchanged with g++ against a fake ESP-IDF TWAI driver and feeds it LK frames. 54 checks: torque packing in the 0x280 frame (motor 1 bytes 0-1, motor 2 mirrored, clamp ±2048), reply parsing (temperature, current, speed, direction), the 0x88/0x80 echoes and foreign IDs ignored, encoder unwrap forwards and backwards for 14/15/16-bit encoders, range detection from the wrap and from the speed ratio, a 100 ms reply gap while the wheel keeps turning, the CAN timeout (including a reply stamped after `now`), a full TX queue never blocking. They found two problems, both fixed: motion before the encoder range is known was counted at the 16-bit guess (now learned after 90° instead of 180°: at most a 1.2 rad one-off offset, no jump), and a reply gap could be taken for an encoder wrap and switch the range (now unwrapped using the reported speed). ## 2. Bench with a USB-CAN adapter (no motors, no battery) Hardware: the ESP32-S3 DevKit + the Waveshare CAN board wired as on the robot (GPIO4 -> CTX, GPIO5 -> CRX, 3.3 V, GND) and a USB-CAN adapter: a candleLight / CANable (gs_usb firmware, ~€15-30) works on Linux (SocketCAN), macOS and Windows (`gs_usb`); a CANable with slcan firmware works everywhere (`slcan:`). Adapter CAN_H/CAN_L/GND to the CAN board's H/L/GND, termination ON at the adapter (the CAN board has its own 120 ohm): ~60 ohm between H and L. ``` pip install python-can pyserial mujoco numpy # + gs_usb on macOS/Windows with a candleLight sudo ip link set can0 up type can bitrate 1000000 # Linux SocketCAN only ``` ### 2a. Transceiver self-test and bus scan (CAN probe firmware) ``` cd firmware/esp32 && pio run -e esp32s3_canprobe -t upload && pio device monitor -e esp32s3_canprobe ``` Prints `self-test: 20/20 frames came back through the transceiver`: the ESP32 sends frames to itself through the SN65HVD230 (no other node needed). 0/20 = CTX/CRX swapped, no 3.3 V or a bad joint. Then it scans IDs 1-4 every 2 s. ### 2b. Watch the robot firmware's traffic Flash the robot firmware (`pio run -e esp32s3 -t upload`) and run ``` python3 bench/can_monitor.py socketcan:can0 ``` Disarmed: 0x9C requests to 0x141/0x142 at ~480/s each, with a 0x80 every 50 ms; nothing answers yet (the adapter ACKs the frames). Error frames must stay at 0. The adapter must be the only extra node. ### 2c. The robot firmware against two virtual motors over the real bus ``` cd firmware/esp32 && pio run -e esp32s3_bench -t upload # robot firmware, IMU from the PC python3 bench/bench_hil.py --serial /dev/ttyUSB0 --can socketcan:can0 ``` `esp32s3_bench` is the robot firmware with the real TWAI driver; only the IMU comes from the PC (DevKit **UART** USB port, 921600, the Pi's arm/drive commands share it). The PC plays motors 1 and 2 on the real bus, runs the physics and feeds the IMU, so the robot stands up, balances, drives, gets pushed - with the real CAN driver, transceiver, wiring, termination and 1 Mbit/s timing. Same scenarios and output as the QEMU test (`hil/run_hil.py`). `can_loss` mutes the virtual motors for 100 ms; also pull the CAN cable by hand while it balances: the firmware must log `motor fault: no CAN reply for ~20 ms`, disarm, and keep sending 0x80. `bench/test_bench.py` checks the kit itself without hardware (virtual CAN bus + the bench build in QEMU). ## 3. One real motor, wheel off the ground 1. With LK's PC tool on the motor's UART connector: ID 1 (left) or 2 (right), CAN 1 Mbit/s. 2. Motor on its supply (or the battery through the 30 A fuse), CAN board H/L to the motor, 60 ohm H-L with power off. 3. CAN probe firmware (2a): the scan must show `motor 1: state ... enc ...`. 4. `e`: turn the wheel one full turn by hand -> counts per turn (cross-check of the firmware's own detection). 5. `+`: 0.2 N·m for 0.5 s. If the wheel turned so the robot would roll forward, keep `DIR_LEFT = +1`, else -1. Same with `2` for the right motor and `DIR_RIGHT`. 6. Only then the robot firmware: boot log `encoder range detected: N counts/turn` once the wheel has turned.

Same scenarios as hil/run_hil.py (QEMU), but with the real TWAI driver, transceiver, wiring, termination and timing. python3 bench_hil.py --serial /dev/ttyUSB0 --can socketcan:can0 [scenario ...] [--seeds 1,2,3] scenarios: standup_face standup_back balance_push drive cmd_timeout can_loss (default: all) Wiring: DevKit "UART" port -> PC (serial), CAN board H/L -> adapter CAN_H/CAN_L + GND, 120 ohm at the adapter end (most adapters have a switch/jumper) and the 120 ohm already on the Waveshare board. continue if t == ord("S") and sim_crc(body) == c: t_us, = struct.unpack("<I", p) w0 = time.perf_counter() with self.lock: dt = CTRL_DT if P.t_fw is None else ((t_us - P.t_fw) & 0xFFFFFFFF) * 1e-6 P.t_fw = t_us if self.cycles > 0: P.advance(min(dt, 0.05)); self.dts.append(dt) self.cycles += 1 imu = P.imu() self.write(sim_frame(ord("I"), imu)) self.host_ms.append(1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - w0)) del buf[:n]; continue del buf[:2] # not a frame: resync # -------------------------------------------------- scenario API (same as run_hil.Host) def run_for(self, seconds, **cmd): t_end = self.plant.t + seconds; deadline = time.time() + seconds * 5 + 20 while self.plant.t < t_end and time.time() < deadline: if cmd.get("silent") is not True: self.link.send(**{k: v for k, v in cmd.items() if k != "silent"}) self.telem.append((self.plant.t, self.link.telem)) time.sleep(0.05) return self.plant.t >= t_end def wait_boot(self, timeout=15): t0 = time.time() while time.time() - t0 < timeout: if any("state" in e for _, e in self.events): return True time.sleep(0.05) return False def main(): ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter) ap.add_argument("--serial", required=True, help="DevKit UART port, e.g. /dev/ttyUSB0, COM4, socket://host:port") ap.add_argument("--can", required=True, help="adapter, e.g. socketcan:can0, gs_usb:0, slcan:/dev/ttyACM0 (see canbus.py)") ap.add_argument("--seeds", default="1") ap.add_argument("--no-reset", action="store_true", help="don't reset the ESP32 through RTS before each scenario") ap.add_argument("--out", default="bench_results.json") ap.add_argument("scenarios", nargs="*") a = ap.parse_args() CFG.update(serial=a.serial, can=a.can, reset=not a.no_reset) run_hil.Host = BenchHost # the scenarios now drive the real ESP32 names = a.scenarios or list(run_hil.SCEN) res = {} for n in names: for s in [int(x) for x in a.seeds.split(",")]: t0 = time.time(); r = run_hil.SCEN[n](s); r["wall_s"] = round(time.time() - t0, 1) res[f"{n}_{s}"] = r print(n, s, json.dumps(r), flush=True) pathlib.Path(a.out).write_text(json.dumps(res, indent=1)) if __name__ == "__main__": main()

"""Watch the robot's CAN bus and decode the LK traffic, once per second. python3 can_monitor.py socketcan:can0 (see canbus.py for other adapters) Per second: frames per ID, the torque the ESP32 commands (0x280, in N·m per motor), the motors' replies (temperature, current, speed, encoder), error frames and the bus load. What to expect from the robot firmware: disarmed : 0x141/0x142 0x9C requests at ~480/s each, every 25th cycle 0x80 instead; replies 0x9C from both motors armed : 0x280 torque at 500/s + 0xA1 replies from 0x141 and 0x142 at 500/s each bus load : ~40 % armed at 1 Mbit/s (3 frames per 2 ms) """ import collections, struct, sys, time from canbus import open_bus KT, IQ_FULL, IQ_MAX = 0.14, 16.5, 2048 BITS_PER_FRAME = 130 # standard 8-byte frame incl. typical bit stuffing def iq_nm(v): return v * IQ_FULL / IQ_MAX * KT def main(spec, seconds=None): bus = open_bus(spec) t0 = last = time.time() cnt = collections.Counter(); errs = 0; latest = {}; total = 0 print(f"listening on {spec} (Ctrl-C to stop)") try: while seconds is None or time.time() - t0 < seconds: m = bus.recv(0.05) if m is not None: total += 1 if m.is_error_frame: errs += 1 else: cmd = m.data[0] if m.dlc else None cnt[(m.arbitration_id, cmd if m.arbitration_id != 0x280 else "iq")] += 1 latest[(m.arbitration_id, cmd)] = bytes(m.data) if time.time() - last >= 1.0: dt = time.time() - last; last = time.time() line = [f"{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')} load {100 * sum(cnt.values()) * BITS_PER_FRAME / 1e6 / dt:4.1f} % errors {errs}"] for (i, c), n in sorted(cnt.items(), key=lambda x: (x[0][0], str(x[0][1]))): tag = "torque 0x280" if i == 0x280 else f"0x{i:03X} {c:#04x}" line.append(f" {tag}: {n / dt:5.0f}/s") for (i, c), d in sorted(latest.items(), key=lambda x: (x[0][0], x[0][1] or 0)): if i == 0x280 and len(d) >= 4: a, b = struct.unpack("<hh", d[:4]); line.append(f" cmd: motor1 {iq_nm(a):+.3f} N·m motor2 {iq_nm(b):+.3f} N·m") elif c in (0x9C, 0xA1) and len(d) == 8 and 0x140 < i < 0x145: t, iq, dps, enc = struct.unpack("<bhhH", d[1:]) line.append(f" motor {i - 0x140}: {t} C {iq * IQ_FULL / IQ_MAX:+.2f} A {dps:+5d} dps enc {enc}") print("\n".join(line), flush=True) cnt.clear(); errs = 0; latest.clear() except KeyboardInterrupt: pass finally: bus.shutdown() return total if __name__ == "__main__": if len(sys.argv) < 2: print(__doc__); sys.exit(1) main(sys.argv[1], float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None)

"""Open a CAN adapter with python-can from a short spec string. socketcan:can0 Linux SocketCAN (candleLight/CANable with gs_usb firmware, PEAK, Kvaser...): first `sudo ip link set can0 up type can bitrate 1000000` gs_usb:0 candleLight/CANable (gs_usb firmware) directly over libusb (macOS, Windows): pip install gs_usb slcan:/dev/ttyACM0 CANable with slcan firmware (any OS), e.g. slcan:COM5 on Windows pcan:PCAN_USBBUS1 PEAK PCAN-USB virtual:test python-can's in-process virtual bus (tests) """ import can BITRATE = 1_000_000 def open_bus(spec): kind, _, chan = spec.partition(":") kw = dict(interface=kind, channel=chan or None) if kind == "gs_usb": kw["channel"] = int(chan or 0); kw["index"] = int(chan or 0); kw["bitrate"] = BITRATE elif kind in ("slcan", "pcan", "kvaser", "ixxat", "vector"): kw["bitrate"] = BITRATE elif kind == "virtual": kw["receive_own_messages"] = False return can.Bus(**kw)

"""Self-test of the bench kit without hardware. 1. CAN side: BenchHost's virtual motors on python-can's in-process virtual bus; a second bus endpoint plays the ESP32 and sends the robot firmware's frames (0x9C, 0x88, 0x280, 0x80, 0xA1); replies are checked byte by byte. 2. Serial side: the bench firmware (env esp32s3_bench_qemu = esp32s3_bench with DIO flash) runs in QEMU; bench_hil talks to its UART0 over TCP exactly as it would over the DevKit's USB-UART: IMU lock-step, Pi command frames (arm) in, telemetry + events out. QEMU has no CAN bus, so the motors never answer: the firmware must arm, try to switch the motors on and report a motor fault (that is the expected end state here). Run: python3 test_bench.py (part 2 needs QEMU + /tmp/flash_bench.bin, see bench/README.md) """ import os, socket, struct, subprocess, sys, time, pathlib HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE)); sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE.parent / "hil")) import can import bench_hil as B from lkbus import ID_L, ID_R, ID_MULTI, DIR, IQ_MAX fails = 0 def check(c, msg): global fails print((" ok " if c else " FAIL ") + msg) if not c: fails += 1 def can_side(): print("1. virtual motors on a python-can bus") B.CFG.update(serial="loop://", can="virtual:benchtest", reset=False) h = B.BenchHost(seed=3); h.plant.place(0) h.start("cantest") esp = can.Bus(interface="virtual", channel="benchtest") def xfer(i, d, n): esp.send(can.Message(arbitration_id=i, data=bytes(d), is_extended_id=False)) out = [] t0 = time.time() while len(out) < n and time.time() - t0 < 1: m = esp.recv(0.1) if m: out.append(m) return out r = xfer(ID_L, [0x9C, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], 1) check(len(r) == 1 and r[0].arbitration_id == ID_L and r[0].data[0] == 0x9C and r[0].dlc == 8, "0x9C read state -> one 0x9C reply from 0x141") r = xfer(ID_R, [0x88, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], 1) check(len(r) == 1 and bytes(r[0].data) == bytes([0x88] + [0] * 7) and h.plant.on[ID_R], "0x88 -> echo of the command, motor 2 on") r = xfer(ID_L, [0x88, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], 1) r = xfer(ID_MULTI, list(struct.pack("<hhhh", 300, -300, 0, 0)), 2) ids = sorted(m.arbitration_id for m in r) check(ids == [ID_L, ID_R] and all(m.data[0] == 0xA1 for m in r), "0x280 -> 0xA1 replies from 0x141 and 0x142") check(h.plant.iq_cmd[ID_L] == 300 and h.plant.iq_cmd[ID_R] == -300, "0x280 iq applied to motor 1 / motor 2") rep = {m.arbitration_id: struct.unpack("<BbhhH", bytes(m.data)) for m in r} check(rep[ID_L][2] == 300 and rep[ID_R][2] == -300, "reply iq = commanded iq") xfer(ID_MULTI, list(struct.pack("<hhhh", 5000, -5000, 0, 0)), 2) check(h.plant.iq_cmd[ID_L] == IQ_MAX and h.plant.iq_cmd[ID_R] == -IQ_MAX, "iq clamped to +-2048") r = xfer(ID_L, [0x80, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], 1) check(len(r) == 1 and r[0].data[0] == 0x80 and not h.plant.on[ID_L] and h.plant.iq_cmd[ID_L] == 0, "0x80 -> echo, motor 1 off, torque 0") h.can_mute_until = h.plant.t + 10 r = xfer(ID_L, [0x9C, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], 1) check(len(r) == 0, "muted (CAN unplugged): no reply") esp.shutdown(); h.close() def serial_side(): print("2. bench firmware in QEMU <-> bench_hil over UART0") flash = "/tmp/flash_bench.bin" if not os.path.exists(flash): print(" skipped: build env esp32s3_bench_qemu into /tmp/flash_bench.bin first"); return s = socket.socket(); s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); port = s.getsockname()[1]; s.close() q = subprocess.Popen([os.environ.get("QEMU", "/opt/dl/qemu/qemu/bin/qemu-system-xtensa"), "-nographic", "-accel", "tcg", "-machine", "esp32s3", "-icount", "shift=2,sleep=on,align=off", "-m", "8M", "-global", "ssi_psram.is_octal=true", "-global", "ssi_psram.size_mbytes=8", "-drive", f"file={flash},if=mtd,format=raw", "-serial", f"tcp:127.0.0.1:{port},server=on,wait=on,nodelay=on", "-monitor", "none"], stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL) time.sleep(1.0) try: B.CFG.update(serial=f"socket://127.0.0.1:{port}", can="virtual:qemutest", reset=False) h = B.BenchHost(seed=1); h.plant.place(0); h.plant.hold = h.plant.d.qpos.copy() h.start("serialtest") booted = h.wait_boot(60) check(booted, "boot: IMU answered over the shared port, state event received as a Pi frame") h.run_for(0.4, arm=False) cyc0 = h.cycles h.run_for(1.0, arm=True) import numpy as np d = np.array(h.dts[-200:]) if h.dts else np.array([0]) check(h.cycles - cyc0 > 300, f"lock-step running: {h.cycles - cyc0} control cycles in 1 s of robot time") check(abs(float(np.median(d)) - 0.002) < 0.0002, f"control period {1e3 * float(np.median(d)):.2f} ms") check(h.link.telem.t_ms > 0, f"telemetry frames parsed (t_ms {h.link.telem.t_ms})") check(h.link.telem.armed, "arm command reached the firmware (armed flag in telemetry)") ev = " | ".join(e for _, e in h.events) check("motor fault" in ev, "no motors on the bus -> firmware reports a CAN motor fault: " + ev[-160:]) h.close() finally: q.terminate(); q.wait(5) if __name__ == "__main__": can_side() serial_side() print(f"\n{'all passed' if not fails else f'{fails} FAILED'}") sys.exit(1 if fails else 0)
