#!/usr/bin/env bash # The whole stair-nod loop, in order. Mirrors ml/run_training.sh for the stand-up. # # ml/run_stairs_training.sh [--steps 800000] # # The gate is ml/evaluate_stairs.py on held-out seeds (20000+), never the eval reward in TensorBoard: # the per-episode reward here is nearly bimodal (the riser comes out or it does not), which is exactly # the signal that made best.zip useless for the stand-up. So every candidate is scored, and the winner # is reported - if none of them beats the scripted baseline, the baseline is what the robot should use. set -eu cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." PY=".venv/bin/python" [ -x "$PY" ] || PY="python3" STEPS=800000 [ "${1:-}" = "--steps" ] && STEPS="$2" echo "== the library the environment runs (the controller is in the loop, so this must be current)" core/build_lib.sh echo echo "== baseline: the hand-scripted nod, on the held-out seeds" "$PY" ml/evaluate_stairs.py --trials 30 --sweep echo echo "== train ($STEPS steps)" "$PY" ml/train_stairs.py --steps "$STEPS" echo echo "== score every candidate on the gate, not on best.zip" BESTN="-1"; WINNER="" for CAND in ml/runs/stairs/best.zip ml/runs/stairs/latest.zip ml/runs/stairs/ckpt/*.zip; do [ -f "$CAND" ] || continue N="$("$PY" ml/evaluate_stairs.py "$CAND" --trials 30 | sed -nE 's/^ randomised stairs *([0-9.]+).*/\1/p')" [ -n "$N" ] || continue echo " $CAND -> success $N" # integer compare in shell: scale the rate by 100 NI="$(printf '%.0f' "$(echo "$N * 100" | bc -l)")" if [ "$NI" -gt "$BESTN" ]; then BESTN="$NI"; WINNER="$CAND"; fi done echo echo "== winner: ${WINNER:-none} (success ${BESTN}%)" [ -n "$WINNER" ] && "$PY" ml/evaluate_stairs.py "$WINNER" --trials 40 --sweep

#!/usr/bin/env bash # The whole learned stand-up loop (ml/README.md), in order: # baseline -> train -> evaluate -> export to C++ -> REBUILD THE LIBRARY -> evaluate what the robot runs. # # ml/run_training.sh # 2,000,000 steps # ml/run_training.sh --steps 500000 # ml/run_training.sh --resume ml/runs/standup/latest.zip # ml/run_training.sh --steps 50000 --no-baseline # quick smoke run # # The rebuild before the last step is the one that is easy to forget by hand: without it # `evaluate.py --compiled` silently measures the PREVIOUS policy and looks like a real result. # # Writes: ml/runs/standup/ (checkpoints, best.zip, TensorBoard logs) and core/standup_policy.hpp. # Progress while it trains: tensorboard --logdir ml/runs set -euo pipefail cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." PY="$PWD/.venv/bin/python"; [ -x "$PY" ] || PY="$(command -v python3)" STEPS=2000000 BASELINE=1 RESUME=() while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do case "$1" in --steps) STEPS="$2"; shift 2 ;; --resume) RESUME=(--resume "$2"); shift 2 ;; --no-baseline) BASELINE=0; shift ;; -h|--help) sed -n '2,15p' "$0"; exit 0 ;; *) echo "unknown option: $1" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac done BEST=ml/runs/standup/best.zip step() { printf '\n\033[1m== %s\033[0m\n' "$1"; } if [ "$BASELINE" = 1 ]; then step "baseline: the hand-tuned stand-up" "$PY" ml/evaluate.py fi step "training $STEPS steps" "$PY" ml/train.py --steps "$STEPS" ${RESUME[@]+"${RESUME[@]}"} # train.py only writes best.zip once EvalCallback has fired (every ~100k steps), although it # always prints that it did. Short runs have latest.zip only. if [ ! -f "$BEST" ]; then BEST=ml/runs/standup/latest.zip [ -f "$BEST" ] || { echo "training produced no model in ml/runs/standup/" >&2; exit 1; } echo "note: no best.zip yet (too few steps for an evaluation) - using $BEST" fi # Which checkpoint? EvalCallback writes best.zip by eval REWARD, and that metric is far too noisy # here to rank anything (sigma ~2.5 on a mean of ~8). One run's "best" was a 100k-step checkpoint # that scored 26/60 compiled while the same run's 2M-step policy scored 171/180 - and it was # exported and reported as the result. So score the candidates on the gate metric itself. score_of() { # -> "<successes out of 60>" for the policy currently in the library # sed, not awk: BSD awk (macOS) has no 3-argument match(), so a gawk-ism would silently # score every candidate 0 here and the choice below would be made on nothing. "$PY" ml/evaluate.py --compiled \ | sed -nE 's#^compiled.*face-down ([0-9]+)/30.*back-down ([0-9]+)/30.*#\1 \2#p' \ | { read -r a b; echo $((a + b)); } } BESTN=-1; WINNER=""; SEEN="" # SEEN must exist before the case below: set -u is on for CAND in "$BEST" ml/runs/standup/latest.zip; do [ -f "$CAND" ] || continue case " $SEEN " in *" $CAND "*) continue ;; esac # --steps < ~100k makes BEST == latest.zip SEEN="$SEEN $CAND" step "scoring $(basename "$CAND") as the C++ controller runs it" "$PY" ml/export_policy.py "$CAND" >/dev/null core/build_lib.sh >/dev/null N="$(score_of)" || N="" [ -n "$N" ] || { echo " $CAND: could not be scored (evaluate.py printed no 'compiled' line)" >&2; continue; } echo " $CAND: $N/60" if [ "$N" -gt "$BESTN" ]; then BESTN="$N"; WINNER="$CAND"; fi done [ -n "$WINNER" ] || { echo "no checkpoint could be scored" >&2; exit 1; } step "exporting the winner ($(basename "$WINNER"), $BESTN/60) to core/standup_policy.hpp" "$PY" ml/export_policy.py "$WINNER" core/build_lib.sh firmware/esp32/sync_core.sh step "learned vs hand-tuned, policy run from Python" "$PY" ml/evaluate.py "$WINNER" step "the policy inside the C++ controller: what the robot will actually run" "$PY" ml/evaluate.py --compiled echo echo "If the two blocks above disagree by more than a couple of robots, the policy is sitting on a" echo "knife edge: the C++ and torch forward passes differ by ~1e-7 and that is enough to flip it." echo "Only the --compiled number is the gate." cat <<'NEXT' Done. core/standup_policy.hpp now holds the trained policy. If --compiled does not clearly beat the hand-tuned stand-up, keep standup_mode = 0: git checkout -- core/standup_policy.hpp && core/build_lib.sh To put it on the robot, see "On the robot" in ml/README.md. NEXT

"""The hand-scripted nod, and the grid that tuned it: the baseline the learned policy has to beat. Four numbers: approach at V_APP, brake one stopping distance before D_DIVE, command -V_REV, and flick to PITCH once the robot is really reversing. Why that shape - and why a flick rather than a held lean - is measured in sim/stairs_probe.py and quoted at the top of ml/stairs_env.py. The trigger is on SPEED, not on distance: a flick entered while still rolling forwards does not just travel further, it diverges (the body is still pitched forward when the balance law takes it back, the catch saturates and the wheels run away past the 114 rad/s guard). Reversing first is not an optimisation, it is the manoeuvre. Everything runs through the environment itself, so the baseline and the policy are scored by exactly the same simulator, noise, estimator and reward. The script only ever uses one of its three nods: it has no way to decide whether a reading was any good, which is one of the things the policy can learn. python ml/stairs_baseline.py --grid # search the recipe (fixed 100 x 300 mm steps) python ml/stairs_baseline.py --trials 20 # score the chosen recipe on randomised staircases """ import argparse, math, pathlib, sys import numpy as np sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent)) from stairs_env import (StairsLookEnv, HOLD, CTRL_DT, V_MAX, NOD_LO, NOD_HI, # noqa: E402 SWING_END_LO, SWING_END_HI) BEST = dict(v_app=0.30, d_dive=0.40, v_rev=0.40, pitch=0.75) BRAKE_EFF = 0.9 # m/s^2 actually achieved when braking: max_accel limits the speed REFERENCE, REACT = 0.10 # s, and the lean that delivers it takes about this long to build up. class Scripted: """Three phases: approach, turn around, flick. Why this is a learning problem and not a geometry problem --------------------------------------------------------- `sim/stairs_probe.py` measured the geometry kinematically (the robot placed at a pitch, nothing balancing). The first tread is visible from a narrow diagonal band of (standoff, pitch), and the riser comes out of it at 101 +- 1 mm against a true 100: standoff 800 700 600 500 450 400 350 300 250 mm pitch -- -- -- 26 26-32 29-35 32-41 35-47 38-50 deg Nothing at all beyond ~550 mm: to see past the step nose the scan plane has to drop below the landing at the edge, tan(theta) > h_lidar / D, and the ray that clears the nose from 800 mm already overflies the whole first tread and lands two steps down. That is why `sim/stairs_look.py`, flying the real controller, got the EDGE right (1.170 +- 55 mm against 1.200) and the riser wrong (88 +- 183 mm): not a sensing failure, a timing failure. Its reverse run-up was 1.5 s long and left the robot 640-1015 mm out when the pitch peaked, in the blind regime. And the timing is not free. A two-wheel balancer cannot hold a pitch standing still - leaning forward IS accelerating forward - so the lean has to be a nod, and gravity acting over the time the body is tilted adds up. `sim/stairs_probe.py` part C2 measures what one costs, over randomised robots, with the real controller flying (a flick: look_time 0, so the depth is the target alone): entry speed target peak travel to peak travel in total upright +0.38 m/s 0.80 34.5 deg +109 mm +1332 mm 0% 0.00 m/s 0.80 34.5 deg +9 mm +1043 mm 100% -0.27 m/s 0.80 34.6 deg -92 mm +441 mm 100% -0.53 m/s 0.80 34.7 deg -169 mm +98 mm 100% -0.53 m/s 0.60 23.9 deg -142 mm +0 mm 100% -0.53 m/s 1.00 46.2 deg -185 mm +880 mm 100% Three things in that table, all of them constraints on the policy: entering the nod REVERSING is what pays for it (the nod's own acceleration cancels the reverse speed and the robot ends up where it started), entering it rolling FORWARDS loses the robot outright, and the depth has to be matched to the standoff because deep nods cost travel while shallow ones see nothing. So the policy has to arrive at a particular standoff with a particular speed and pick a depth to match, with the whole manoeuvre fitting in the landing it has left. Nothing about that is a lookup table. What it is up against: a hand-scripted version of exactly that recipe (ml/stairs_baseline.py, tuned by grid search) measures the riser to 3 +- 5 mm on the 100 x 300 mm staircase it was tuned on, and 40% on randomised ones - because one fixed depth cannot cover 80 to 170 mm of riser. It gets 0/10 at 170 mm. The episode ----------- The robot starts upright and balancing, 0.70-1.40 m from the edge, on a staircase whose riser (80-170 mm) and tread (240-320 mm) are drawn fresh every episode, with the usual randomised robot (mass, CoM, inertia, tyre grip, battery, torque gain, CAN delay, IMU bias and mount tilt). It already knows roughly where the edge is: the probe showed the EDGE is recoverable from any standoff (-3 mm at 800 mm), so a reconnaissance nod from far back is not simulated - the environment hands the policy that estimate with the measured noise (EDGE_SD) instead, and the policy tracks it with wheel odometry. The riser is what nobody can get from far away, and it is the only thing rewarded. Every 50 ms the policy chooses a wheel speed, and whether to nod now and how deep. It gets MAX_NODS nods (one - see the note on the constant), costing NOD_COST, and keeps whichever produced the most confident reading: most returns on the surface it measured the riser from, which is a number the robot has. The reward is paid as the improvement in that best reading, so the nod that found it gets credit. A speed command that would drive at the drop from inside D_FENCE is refused - see that constant. Observation (8 floats, all of them things the real robot has): d_est / 1.5 distance to the edge: the reconnaissance estimate minus wheel odometry v / V_MAX odometry speed, + = towards the edge pitch rad, the controller's own estimate 0.1 * pitch rate t / T_MAX time used nods / MAX_NODS confidence min(returns on the measured surface / 400, 1): 0 until something has been measured last action the speed command of the previous step (one CAN period of latency) Action (3 floats in [-1, 1]): v command = V_MAX * a0 m/s; nod now if a1 > 0 (and only inside D_ARM); depth NOD_LO..NOD_HI from a2. """Gymnasium environment: learn the stand-up (lying -> upright) with the real controller in the loop. The robot lies on its face or back (random side), the C++ controller detects the side, waits until it is still and starts the push (state LIFT). From there the policy sets the push every 10 ms (`standup_mode = 2`: torque from outside) until the controller's normal catch takes over (|pitch| < 20°) or it gives up. After the catch the episode keeps running 1 s under the normal balance controller: success = still balancing, upright, without running off. Every episode uses a randomised robot (mass, centre of mass, inertia, tyre grip, battery voltage, torque gain, CAN delay, IMU bias and mount): the same randomisation as sim/run_tests.py, so the policy doesn't overfit one robot. Curriculum: the first run (2 M steps, ent_coef 0) never found the success bonus - it half-rose, ran out the controller's 2 s timeout and collected the shaping, and once the exploration noise had annealed away it could no longer discover anything better. So training starts nearer upright and each worker walks its own start pitch out to the real 1.8 rad as it succeeds. Evaluation always uses the real task: StandupEnv(curriculum=False). What the ratchet is gated on matters, and the third run got it wrong: it advanced only on a full success (caught first try AND still balancing a second later), which sat around 12%, never reached UP_OK, and so left every worker pinned at PITCH_START for all 2 M steps. The curriculum silently collapsed to "always train at 1.2 rad". It is now gated on a catchable handover - a success, or reaching the catch with `gentle` >= GENTLE_OK (pitch rate <= ~6.7 rad/s). That is the thing the reward is pushing for, it is reached early in training, and it gets harder as the start pitch grows, so the ratchet has signal to climb on and self-limits. The strict success rate is still reported separately (env/success_rate vs env/curric_rate). The catch is a handover, not a finish line. The second run (flat CATCH_ONLY = +2.0) reached the catch window on every episode and lost every one of them: measured in ml/evaluate.py's loop it arrived at |pitch rate| 16.9 rad/s median against the hand-tuned stand-up's 3.66. Both swing up equally hard (peak ~14-17 rad/s in the 150 ms before the catch); the hand-tuned one *decelerates into the window*, the learned one is still at its peak when it crosses. Nothing in the reward mentioned the rate, so the fastest route into the window won and the gradient from 17 rad/s towards 4 was exactly zero. CATCH_ONLY is now scaled by exp(-(rate/RATE_OK)^2): ~0.8 at the hand-tuned arrival, ~0.01 at a slam, monotone in between. The rate is reported in the info dict so it shows up in TensorBoard (env/catch_rate_rad_s) instead of having to be measured afterwards. That rate is differentiated from the simulator's body quaternion, captured at the catch tick. The gyro itself is faithful (corr 1.000 with the truth over the swing, one control tick of lag), so o.pitch_rate would have done - but only if read at the right moment: BotSim.step() returns BotSim.out itself, one ctypes struct the C++ refills in place every tick. Read below the post-catch check loop it reported 5.5 rad/s for a handover that really happened at 16.9, because by then the struct described the robot a second later. Observation (6 floats, side-normalised, computed by the controller itself: Controller::standup_obs): pitch, 0.1·pitch rate, wheel speed / max, time / timeout, (vbat - 23)/2, last action Action: 1 float in [-1, 1] = push for both motors as a fraction of 2 × torque_limit (4.6 N·m). """ import collections, sys, math, pathlib, ctypes as C import numpy as np import gymnasium as gym ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "sim")) from botsim import BotSim, LIB, CTRL_DT, quat_pitch # noqa: E402 LIFT, BALANCE = 2, 4 HOLD = 5 # control ticks per policy step (= STANDUP_HOLD in core/standup_policy.hpp) NOBS = 6 CHECK_AFTER_CATCH = 1.0 # s of normal balancing that must follow a catch SHAPE = 5.0 # weight of the progress-towards-upright shaping CATCH_ONLY = 2.0 # reached the catch but the balance controller lost it (scaled by how gently) RATE_OK = 8.0 # rad/s: pitch rate at the catch that still earns most of CATCH_ONLY FALLEN_PENALTY = -2.0 # went over, ran away or gave up (was -5: too timid to explore) PITCH_FULL = 1.8 # rad: lying flat, the real task PITCH_START = 1.2 # rad: where the curriculum begins PITCH_STEP = 0.05 # rad moved per adjustment WINDOW = 20 # episodes the curriculum signal is measured over UP_OK, UP_BAD = 0.6, 0.3 # rate of that signal that makes the task harder / easier GENTLE_OK = 0.5 # `gentle` (i.e. rate <= 6.7 rad/s) that counts as a catchable handover class StandupEnv(gym.Env): metadata = {"render_modes": []} def __init__(self, seed=None, fixed_side=None, curriculum=True): self.observation_space = gym.spaces.Box(-5.0, 5.0, (NOBS,), np.float32) self.action_space = gym.spaces.Box(-1.0, 1.0, (1,), np.float32) self.sim = None self.fixed_side = fixed_side self._obs = (C.c_float * NOBS)() # each worker carries its own curriculum: no plumbing through SubprocVecEnv self.curriculum = curriculum self.pitch = PITCH_START if curriculum else PITCH_FULL self.recent = collections.deque(maxlen=WINDOW) def _advance_curriculum(self, good): """Walk the start pitch towards PITCH_FULL while handovers are catchable, back off while they are not.""" if not self.curriculum: return self.recent.append(bool(good)) if len(self.recent) < WINDOW: return rate = sum(self.recent) / len(self.recent) if rate >= UP_OK and self.pitch < PITCH_FULL: self.pitch = min(PITCH_FULL, self.pitch + PITCH_STEP); self.recent.clear() elif rate <= UP_BAD and self.pitch > PITCH_START: self.pitch = max(PITCH_START, self.pitch - PITCH_STEP); self.recent.clear() def _obs_now(self): LIB.bot_standup_obs(self.sim.ctl, self._obs) return np.array(self._obs, dtype=np.float32) def reset(self, seed=None, options=None): super().reset(seed=seed) if self.sim is not None: self.sim.close() sim_seed = int(self.np_random.integers(0, 2**31 - 1)) if (options or {}).get("sim_seed") is None else options["sim_seed"] side = (options or {}).get("side") or self.fixed_side or (1 if self.np_random.random() < 0.5 else -1) pitch = (options or {}).get("pitch") or self.pitch self.sim = BotSim(seed=sim_seed, randomize=True) self.sim.place(pitch=pitch * side) self.up0 = math.cos(pitch) LIB.bot_standup(self.sim.ctl, 2, 0.0) for _ in range(int(1.5 / CTRL_DT)): # lying: the controller waits until it is still, then starts the push if self.sim.step().state == LIFT: break self.x0 = float(self.sim.d.qpos[0]); self.y0 = float(self.sim.d.qpos[1]) self.prev_up = math.cos(self.sim.out.pitch) self.true_pitch = quat_pitch(self.sim.d.qpos[3:7]) return self._obs_now(), {} def step(self, action): a = float(np.clip(action[0], -1.0, 1.0)) LIB.bot_standup(self.sim.ctl, 2, a * 2 * 2.3) for _ in range(HOLD): prev_true = self.true_pitch o = self.sim.step() self.true_pitch = quat_pitch(self.sim.d.qpos[3:7]) if o.state != LIFT: break true_rate = abs(self.true_pitch - prev_true) / CTRL_DT true_v = abs(float(o.v)) # copy it NOW: see the note on `o` below obs = self._obs_now() # Shaping: progress towards upright, small costs for spinning the wheels fast and for big pushes. # It telescopes to SHAPE * (cos pitch_end - cos pitch_start), so SHAPE sets how much an episode can earn # by rising at all. At 2.0 that was +2.45 against a +10 all-or-nothing bonus the policy never reached; # 5.0 makes partial progress worth chasing without letting it beat an actual stand-up. up = math.cos(o.pitch) r = SHAPE * (up - self.prev_up) - 0.002 * a * a - 0.01 * float(obs[2]) ** 2 self.prev_up = up if o.state == LIFT: return obs, r, False, False, {} if o.state == BALANCE: # caught: does the normal controller keep it? # `o` is BotSim.out itself, one ctypes struct the C++ refills in place on every step, not a # snapshot. Anything about the handover has to be copied before the check loop below steps the # sim on: reading o.pitch_rate after it reported 5.5 rad/s where the catch really saw 16.9. ok = True for _ in range(int(CHECK_AFTER_CATCH / CTRL_DT)): if self.sim.step().state != BALANCE: ok = False; break travel = math.hypot(self.sim.d.qpos[0] - self.x0, self.sim.d.qpos[1] - self.y0) ok = ok and abs(self.sim.out.pitch) < math.radians(12) rate = true_rate # how fast the body really was turning when the catch fired # Reaching the catch is most of the job, so credit it even when the balance controller drops it - # but only in proportion to how catchable the handover was. A slam through the window earns nothing. gentle = math.exp(-(rate / RATE_OK) ** 2) r += (10.0 - 2.0 * travel) if ok else CATCH_ONLY * gentle # Ratchet on a catchable handover, not on a full success: see the note at the top of the file. curric = bool(ok or gentle >= GENTLE_OK) self._advance_curriculum(curric) return obs, r, True, False, {"success": ok, "travel": travel, "catch_rate": rate, "catch_v": true_v, "start_pitch": self.pitch, "curric": curric} self._advance_curriculum(False) # went over, ran away or gave up return obs, r + FALLEN_PENALTY, True, False, {"success": False, "start_pitch": self.pitch, "curric": False} def close(self): if self.sim is not None: self.sim.close(); self.sim = None

"""Train the stand-up policy with PPO (stable-baselines3), one simulator per CPU core. python ml/train.py --steps 2000000 # on a Mac M-series: ~30-60 min (a guess until measured) python ml/train.py --steps 2000000 --resume ml/runs/standup/latest.zip Writes ml/runs/standup/: checkpoints, latest.zip, best.zip (by the periodic evaluation) and TensorBoard logs (`tensorboard --logdir ml/runs`). Then: python ml/evaluate.py, python ml/export_policy.py. """ import argparse, collections, os, pathlib, sys import numpy as np from stable_baselines3 import PPO from stable_baselines3.common.callbacks import BaseCallback, CheckpointCallback, EvalCallback from stable_baselines3.common.env_util import make_vec_env from stable_baselines3.common.vec_env import SubprocVecEnv sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent)) from standup_env import StandupEnv # noqa: E402 OUT = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "runs" / "standup" class EnvStats(BaseCallback): """Rolling means of what the environment is actually doing, logged to TensorBoard. Two 2 M-step runs failed for reasons that were invisible in the PPO scalars: the first never reached the catch, the second reached it far too fast. Both had to be diagnosed afterwards from a separate script. These three numbers would have shown either failure within the first 100 k steps. """ def __init__(self, n=200): super().__init__() self.succ = collections.deque(maxlen=n) self.rate = collections.deque(maxlen=n) self.pitch = collections.deque(maxlen=n) self.v = collections.deque(maxlen=n) self.curric = collections.deque(maxlen=n) def _on_step(self): for i in self.locals.get("infos", ()): if "success" in i: self.succ.append(float(i["success"])) if "catch_rate" in i: self.rate.append(i["catch_rate"]) if "catch_v" in i: self.v.append(i["catch_v"]) if "curric" in i: self.curric.append(float(i["curric"])) if "start_pitch" in i: self.pitch.append(i["start_pitch"]) if self.succ: self.logger.record("env/success_rate", sum(self.succ) / len(self.succ)) if self.rate: self.logger.record("env/catch_rate_rad_s", sum(self.rate) / len(self.rate)) if self.v: self.logger.record("env/catch_v_m_s", sum(self.v) / len(self.v)) if self.curric: self.logger.record("env/curric_rate", sum(self.curric) / len(self.curric)) if self.pitch: self.logger.record("env/start_pitch", sum(self.pitch) / len(self.pitch)) return True def main(): ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=2_000_000, help="policy steps (10 ms each) in total") ap.add_argument("--envs", type=int, default=max(1, (os.cpu_count() or 2) - 1)) ap.add_argument("--resume", type=str, default=None) ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=1) a = ap.parse_args() OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) env = make_vec_env(StandupEnv, n_envs=a.envs, seed=a.seed, vec_env_cls=SubprocVecEnv if a.envs > 1 else None) # evaluation is always the real task: no curriculum, so the eval curve stays comparable across runs eval_env = make_vec_env(StandupEnv, n_envs=1, seed=10_000, env_kwargs=dict(curriculum=False)) if a.resume: model = PPO.load(a.resume, env=env, device="cpu") else: model = PPO("MlpPolicy", env, device="cpu", seed=a.seed, verbose=1, tensorboard_log=str(OUT / "tb"), n_steps=512, batch_size=512, n_epochs=10, gamma=0.995, gae_lambda=0.95, learning_rate=3e-4, ent_coef=0.01, clip_range=0.2, policy_kwargs=dict(net_arch=dict(pi=[64, 64], vf=[64, 64]), log_std_init=0.0)) # ent_coef and log_std_init 0.0: with ent_coef 0 the first run's action noise annealed from std 0.60 # to 0.15 by 1 M steps, the reward stopped improving at 250 k and never recovered. 0.005 was not # enough either (0.97 -> 0.17 over the second run), hence 0.01. # batch_size 512 divides n_steps * n_envs exactly, so no truncated minibatch each update. # small tanh MLP on purpose: it is exported to C++ and runs on the ESP32-S3 every 10 ms cbs = [EnvStats(), CheckpointCallback(save_freq=max(1, 200_000 // a.envs), save_path=str(OUT / "ckpt"), name_prefix="standup"), EvalCallback(eval_env, n_eval_episodes=40, eval_freq=max(1, 100_000 // a.envs), deterministic=True, best_model_save_path=str(OUT), log_path=str(OUT / "eval"))] model.learn(total_timesteps=a.steps, callback=cbs, reset_num_timesteps=a.resume is None) model.save(OUT / "latest") os.replace(OUT / "best_model.zip", OUT / "best.zip") if (OUT / "best_model.zip").exists() else None print("saved", OUT / "latest.zip", "and", OUT / "best.zip") if __name__ == "__main__": main()

"""Train the step-down policy with PPO, one simulator per core. python ml/train_descend.py --steps 3000000 --envs 12 python ml/train_descend.py --steps 1000000 --resume ml/runs/descend/latest.zip The hand-written recipe it has to beat is in sim/stairs_descend.py: roll at a fixed speed, commit to step_mode a fixed distance before the edge, hold a fixed attitude. Three constants, tuned on a grid, scoring 57% in this environment. The opening is that those constants cannot depend on the step - and the robot knows the riser to about 13 mm before it moves, because the array measured it. What to watch, in this order (all under env/ in TensorBoard): crossed_rate did it step at all. If this collapses to 0 the reward is wrong again: refusing to step is always the safe choice, and NO_STEP exists to make it the wrong one. success_rate landed, settled, and stayed settled peak_deg how far the body went over. The recipe runs at 8-12 deg; a tumble is 46. fell_rate / ran_on_rate the two ways it loses: on its face, or across the tread and off the next Do NOT judge a run by best.zip - see the note in CLAUDE.md, it cost a whole run on the stand-up. ml/evaluate_descend.py scores every checkpoint on held-out staircases, and that is the gate. """ import argparse, collections, os, pathlib, shutil, sys import numpy as np from stable_baselines3 import PPO from stable_baselines3.common.callbacks import BaseCallback, CheckpointCallback from stable_baselines3.common.env_util import make_vec_env from stable_baselines3.common.vec_env import SubprocVecEnv sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent)) from descend_env import DescendEnv, RISE_HI # noqa: E402 OUT = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "runs" / "descend" KEYS = ("success", "fell", "ran_on", "no_step", "crossed", "peak_deg", "rise_mm", "t_end", "committed", "end_pitch_deg") class Curriculum(BaseCallback): """Raise the tallest riser once the policy can handle the ones it is getting. Ratchets on SUCCESS, not on crossing: a gate that advances on merely stepping would hand the policy taller and taller steps it cannot land, which is how the stand-up's curriculum silently stalled for 2 M steps. It never goes back down, and it stops at the real distribution. """ def __init__(self, stats, start=0.07, step=0.015, up_at=0.55, window=300, every=5000): super().__init__() self.stats, self.hi, self.step, self.up_at = stats, start, step, up_at self.window, self.every = window, every def _on_step(self): if self.n_calls % self.every or self.hi >= RISE_HI - 1e-6: return True d = self.stats.buf["success"] if len(d) >= self.window and float(np.mean(d)) > self.up_at: self.hi = min(RISE_HI, self.hi + self.step) self.training_env.env_method("set_rise_hi", self.hi) d.clear() print(f" curriculum -> risers up to {self.hi*1000:.0f} mm") self.logger.record("env/curriculum_rise_hi_mm", self.hi * 1000) return True class EnvStats(BaseCallback): """Rolling means of every info key, so a bad reward shows up in minutes rather than at the end.""" def __init__(self, window=200): super().__init__() self.buf = {k: collections.deque(maxlen=window) for k in KEYS} def _on_step(self): for info in self.locals.get("infos", []): if "success" not in info: continue for k in KEYS: if k in info: self.buf[k].append(float(info[k])) if self.n_calls % 500 == 0: for k, d in self.buf.items(): if d: name = f"env/{k}" + ("_rate" if k in ("success", "fell", "ran_on", "no_step", "crossed", "committed") else "") self.logger.record(name, float(np.mean(d))) return True def main(): ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=3_000_000) ap.add_argument("--envs", type=int, default=12) ap.add_argument("--resume", default=None) ap.add_argument("--curriculum", action="store_true", help="start on small risers and ratchet up; pointless from a warm start, which " "already steps on the full distribution") a = ap.parse_args() OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) ck = OUT / "ckpt" if not a.resume and ck.exists(): # checkpoints are named by step count, so a shorter run leaves older, longer-numbered files # behind and the scorer happily picks one from a different reward. Clear them. shutil.rmtree(ck) ck.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) env = make_vec_env(DescendEnv, n_envs=a.envs, vec_env_cls=SubprocVecEnv, env_kwargs=dict(curriculum=a.curriculum)) if a.resume: model = PPO.load(a.resume, env=env, device="cpu") print(f"resumed from {a.resume}") else: model = PPO("MlpPolicy", env, verbose=1, device="cpu", tensorboard_log=str(OUT), n_steps=256, batch_size=512, gamma=0.99, gae_lambda=0.95, learning_rate=3e-4, ent_coef=0.004, clip_range=0.2, policy_kwargs=dict(net_arch=dict(pi=[64, 64], vf=[64, 64]), log_std_init=0.0)) stats = EnvStats() cbs = [stats] + ([Curriculum(stats)] if a.curriculum else []) + [CheckpointCallback(save_freq=max(1, 100_000 // a.envs), save_path=str(ck), name_prefix="descend")] model.learn(total_timesteps=a.steps, callback=cbs, progress_bar=False, reset_num_timesteps=not a.resume) model.save(str(OUT / "latest.zip")) print(f"saved {OUT / 'latest.zip'}") if __name__ == "__main__": main()

"""Train the nod-timing policy with PPO (stable-baselines3), one simulator per CPU core. python ml/train_stairs.py --steps 600000 python ml/train_stairs.py --steps 600000 --resume ml/runs/stairs/latest.zip Writes ml/runs/stairs/: checkpoints, latest.zip, best.zip (by the periodic evaluation) and TensorBoard logs (`tensorboard --logdir ml/runs`). Then: python ml/evaluate_stairs.py ml/runs/stairs/latest.zip. best.zip is NOT to be trusted on its own - see the note in CLAUDE.md. The eval reward here is just as noisy as the stand-up's was (the riser either comes out or it does not, so the per-episode reward is nearly bimodal between 0 and 10), so ml/evaluate_stairs.py scores every candidate on held-out staircases and that is the gate. What to watch, in this order (all under env/ in TensorBoard): start_d0 how far out the episode started (training 0.55-1.30, evaluation 0.70-1.30) measured_rate did the cloud contain the first tread at all - the sensing curric_rate clean readings, which is what the curriculum ratchets on d_peak_mm standoff when the pitch peaked - only indicative, since the nod SWEEPS the band while the robot moves, so the measurement often comes from earlier in the nod rise_err_mm the actual measurement error margin_mm how close to the drop it ended up, and off_edge_rate / fell_rate A run where measured_rate climbs but margin_mm sinks is learning to measure by falling downstairs. """ import argparse, collections, os, pathlib, sys import numpy as np from stable_baselines3 import PPO from stable_baselines3.common.callbacks import BaseCallback, CheckpointCallback, EvalCallback from stable_baselines3.common.env_util import make_vec_env from stable_baselines3.common.vec_env import SubprocVecEnv sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent)) from stairs_env import StairsLookEnv # noqa: E402 OUT = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "runs" / "stairs" KEYS = ("success", "measured", "rise_err_mm", "margin_mm", "d_peak_mm", "peak_deg", "d_best_mm", "peak_best_deg", "fell", "off_edge", "no_nod", "n_pts", "conf", "nods", "t_end", "curric", "start_d0", "n_seen") class EnvStats(BaseCallback): """Rolling means of what the environment is actually doing (NaNs skipped: a missed riser has no error).""" def __init__(self, n=200): super().__init__() self.q = {k: collections.deque(maxlen=n) for k in KEYS} def _on_step(self): for i in self.locals.get("infos", ()): for k in KEYS: v = i.get(k) if v is not None and not (isinstance(v, float) and np.isnan(v)): self.q[k].append(float(v)) for k, d in self.q.items(): if d: name = (k if k.endswith(("_mm", "_deg", "_pts")) or k in ("conf", "nods", "t_end", "start_d0", "n_seen") else k + "_rate") self.logger.record(f"env/{name}", sum(d) / len(d)) return True def main(): ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=600_000, help="policy steps (50 ms each) in total") ap.add_argument("--envs", type=int, default=max(1, (os.cpu_count() or 2) - 1)) ap.add_argument("--resume", type=str, default=None) ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=1) a = ap.parse_args() OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) if not a.resume: # Clear the previous run's artefacts. CheckpointCallback names files by step count, so without # this a new run only overwrites the checkpoints it happens to reach and leaves the older run's # later ones behind - and they load fine, because the spaces have not changed, so a candidate # trained in a DIFFERENT environment gets scored as if it were this run's. One ckpt directory # here held three runs at once, two of them with a different nod budget. stale = sorted((OUT / "ckpt").glob("*.zip")) + [OUT / "best.zip", OUT / "latest.zip", OUT / "best_model.zip"] for f in stale: if f.exists(): f.unlink() if stale: print(f"cleared {sum(1 for f in stale)} stale checkpoint(s) from a previous run") env = make_vec_env(StairsLookEnv, n_envs=a.envs, seed=a.seed, env_kwargs=dict(curriculum=True), vec_env_cls=SubprocVecEnv if a.envs > 1 else None) # evaluation is always the real task (curriculum off by default), so the curve stays comparable eval_env = make_vec_env(StairsLookEnv, n_envs=1, seed=10_000) if a.resume: model = PPO.load(a.resume, env=env, device="cpu") else: model = PPO("MlpPolicy", env, device="cpu", seed=a.seed, verbose=1, tensorboard_log=str(OUT / "tb"), n_steps=256, batch_size=512, n_epochs=10, gamma=0.99, gae_lambda=0.95, learning_rate=3e-4, ent_coef=0.004, clip_range=0.2, policy_kwargs=dict(net_arch=dict(pi=[64, 64], vf=[64, 64]), log_std_init=0.0)) # ent_coef 0.004, not the stand-up's 0.01: that task needed sustained exploration to find a # torque profile at all, this one is a narrow placement choice inside a gated window, and a high # entropy bonus keeps the nod trigger firing early when it should be becoming decisive. # gamma 0.99: an episode is ~30-100 steps of approach and the reward is all at the end, so the # horizon has to cover the whole approach (0.99^100 = 0.37) without being so long that the # per-step time cost disappears. n_steps 256 x envs still gives whole episodes per update. cbs = [EnvStats(), CheckpointCallback(save_freq=max(1, 100_000 // a.envs), save_path=str(OUT / "ckpt"), name_prefix="stairs"), EvalCallback(eval_env, n_eval_episodes=30, eval_freq=max(1, 50_000 // a.envs), deterministic=True, best_model_save_path=str(OUT), log_path=str(OUT / "eval"))] model.learn(total_timesteps=a.steps, callback=cbs, reset_num_timesteps=a.resume is None) model.save(OUT / "latest") if (OUT / "best_model.zip").exists(): os.replace(OUT / "best_model.zip", OUT / "best.zip") print("saved", OUT / "latest.zip") if __name__ == "__main__": main()

"""Warm-start the step-down policy by imitating the hand-written recipe, then let PPO improve it. Starting PPO from noise does not work here and it is worth being precise about why. The recipe is three decisions that have to coincide: roll at a moderate speed, commit within a couple of centimetres of an edge, and stop asking for speed. Miss any one and the robot tumbles. A random policy crosses the edge readily - that part is easy - and lands essentially never, so every early trajectory ends the same way and there is no gradient towards the one combination that works. So this clones the recipe first. It is a few hundred episodes of supervised learning on (observation, action) pairs, which costs minutes and puts the policy somewhere PPO can actually improve from. The recipe scores about 57% in this environment; anything the training does afterwards is measured against that, not against zero. python ml/warmstart_descend.py --episodes 400 python ml/train_descend.py --resume ml/runs/descend/bc.zip --steps 3000000 """ import argparse, pathlib, sys import numpy as np import torch from stable_baselines3 import PPO from stable_baselines3.common.env_util import make_vec_env sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent)) from descend_env import DescendEnv, V_MAX, STEP_LO, STEP_HI # noqa: E402 OUT = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "runs" / "descend" def recipe(obs, state, v_roll=0.20, arm=0.020, hold=0.0): """The tuned recipe as an action: roll, commit just before the edge, then stop asking for speed. Reads only what the robot has - the array's distance estimate - so the demonstrations are reachable by the policy rather than being privileged. """ d = float(obs[0]) * 0.5 if d < 0.0: state["past"] = True v = 0.0 if state.get("past") else v_roll return np.array([2.0 * v / V_MAX - 1.0, 1.0 if d < arm else -1.0, 2.0 * (hold - STEP_LO) / (STEP_HI - STEP_LO) - 1.0], dtype=np.float32) def collect(episodes, seed0=7000, jitter=True): """Demonstrations, with the recipe's own constants jittered a little. Cloning one exact trajectory teaches the policy a single reflex; jittering the speed and the commit distance across episodes shows it the shape of the decision instead, which is what we want it to keep when PPO starts moving it. """ env = DescendEnv(seed=seed0) X, Y, ok = [], [], 0 rng = np.random.default_rng(seed0) for k in range(episodes): obs, _ = env.reset(seed=seed0 + k) v = float(rng.uniform(0.15, 0.26)) if jitter else 0.20 arm = float(rng.uniform(0.012, 0.030)) if jitter else 0.020 hold = float(rng.uniform(-0.04, 0.02)) if jitter else 0.0 st, ep_x, ep_y = {}, [], [] while True: a = recipe(obs, st, v, arm, hold) ep_x.append(np.asarray(obs, dtype=np.float32)); ep_y.append(a) obs, r, done, _, info = env.step(a) if done: break if info["success"]: # clone what WORKED, not what merely happened X += ep_x; Y += ep_y; ok += 1 if (k + 1) % 50 == 0: print(f" {k+1}/{episodes} episodes, {ok} usable ({ok/(k+1):.0%}), {len(X)} samples") env.close() return np.array(X, dtype=np.float32), np.array(Y, dtype=np.float32), ok / max(1, episodes) def main(): ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--episodes", type=int, default=400) ap.add_argument("--epochs", type=int, default=60) a = ap.parse_args() OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) X, Y, rate = collect(a.episodes) print(f"collected {len(X)} samples from {rate:.0%} successful demonstrations") if len(X) < 500: raise SystemExit("too few successful demonstrations to clone - check the recipe constants") env = make_vec_env(DescendEnv, n_envs=1, env_kwargs=dict(curriculum=False)) model = PPO("MlpPolicy", env, device="cpu", n_steps=256, batch_size=512, policy_kwargs=dict(net_arch=dict(pi=[64, 64], vf=[64, 64]), log_std_init=0.0)) pol = model.policy opt = torch.optim.Adam(pol.parameters(), lr=1e-3) xt, yt = torch.as_tensor(X), torch.as_tensor(Y) n = len(xt) for ep in range(a.epochs): perm = torch.randperm(n) tot = 0.0 for i in range(0, n, 256): idx = perm[i:i + 256] feat = pol.extract_features(xt[idx]) if isinstance(feat, tuple): feat = feat[0] mean = pol.action_net(pol.mlp_extractor.forward_actor(feat)) loss = torch.nn.functional.mse_loss(mean, yt[idx]) opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step() tot += float(loss) * len(idx) if ep % 10 == 0 or ep == a.epochs - 1: print(f" epoch {ep:3d} mse {tot/n:.4f}") model.save(str(OUT / "bc.zip")) print(f"saved {OUT / 'bc.zip'}") if __name__ == "__main__": main()

On these {len(ab)}: flick {ab_f}/{len(ab)}, swing {ab_s}/{len(ab)}.</p> <div class="wide">{"".join(pair(r) for r in ab)}</div> <p class="note"><b>What the pairs show that the averages do not.</b> The swing's distinctive failure — the one the flick almost never has, 38% of episodes against 7% — is not a bad number, it is <b>no number</b>: it stops close, pitches down, and every ray clears the landing and lands on the tread. A riser is the difference between two surfaces, so hundreds of returns on the tread measure nothing with no landing left to subtract from. {"One" if ab_blind == 1 else ab_blind} of these ten clips fails exactly that way, with 597 rays on the tread and no number out of them. The flick does not have the problem because it takes its look from further back while reversing, so the landing stays in the scan; what it does instead, when it fails, is overfly the first tread and measure a surface two steps down.</p> <h2>Two ways to take the look</h2> <p class="sub">A <b>flick</b> is one-sided: gravity acts forward for the whole nod, so it costs 0.1–1.1 m of travel towards the drop. A <b>swing</b> leans back for as long as it leans forward, so it travels almost nothing — 650 mm of standoff became 638 mm across six cycles — and its amplitude grows each cycle, because the angle that sees a 170 mm riser is not the one that sees an 80 mm riser and the robot cannot know which it faces until it has measured it.</p> <div class="tw"><table><thead><tr><th>look</th><th>success</th><th>read anything</th><th>riser error</th> <th>landing left</th><th>worst</th><th>fell or went over</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td>one-sided flick</td><td class="m">0.390</td><td class="m">0.93</td> <td class="m">202 ± 297 mm</td><td class="m">207 mm</td><td class="m">−68 mm</td> <td class="m">0.105</td></tr> <tr><td>creep in, then swing</td><td class="m">0.290</td><td class="m">0.62</td> <td class="m">213 ± 299 mm</td><td class="m">249 mm</td><td class="m">−386 mm</td> <td class="m">0.185</td></tr> </tbody></table></div> <p class="note">Same harness, same 200 held-out staircases, seeds 20000 onwards. The flick wins by 10 points, and at 2.1σ over 200 episodes that gap is real — an earlier 30-episode run put it at 14 points, which was 1.2σ and would have settled nothing. <b>The swing loses twice over.</b> It reads nothing at all in 38% of episodes against the flick's 7%, and it goes over the edge <em>more</em> often, 0.155 against 0.080, not less: it creeps to a fixed standoff and never reverses, so a misjudged stop keeps going forward, while backing away from the drop is part of what the flick is doing anyway. On a staircase whose riser is already known it is much the better look — 6 of 6 successes at 5 mm of error on a 100 mm riser, and it barely translates, 650 mm of standoff becoming 638 mm over six cycles. It loses across <em>unknown</em> staircases because the amplitude it can safely reach caps the angle, and a tall riser needs an angle it cannot get to from a standoff it can survive.</p> <p class="note"><b>And it cannot be done from close in.</b> Creeping to 150 mm is safe — the robot gets there without trouble and the swing is stable — and useless: 0 to 3 returns on the first tread, the riser read 469 mm wrong. Closer is worse, not better. The step nose subtends a larger angle the nearer you are, so the pitch needed to see past it rises: 41–50° at 200 mm, roughly 60–70° at 150 mm, while above about 0.8 rad of amplitude the swing loses the robot. The limit is the lidar sitting 231 mm up, not the controller. A cheap time-of-flight sensor at ~80 mm would see the first tread from 600 mm with a 20° nod and make the whole manoeuvre easy.</p> <h2>A sensor that does not need the nod</h2> <p class="sub">Every number above is limited by one thing. A ray reaches the first tread only if it clears the step nose and lands before the next one, which needs <b>D < h × tread / rise</b>, and the landing hides everything below it short of the edge — so the vertical riser face is never visible from behind the edge, at any angle. The limit is the sensor's <b>height</b>. At the lidar's 231 mm a 170 mm riser is out of reach beyond 408 mm; at the sonar's 134 mm, beyond 237 mm. Mounting a depth sensor low would be the worst place for it.</p> <p class="note">A <b>VL53L5CX</b> does not reach further — it obeys the same geometry — it reaches <em>simultaneously</em>. The lidar has one scan plane and has to pitch the whole robot to put that plane inside the band, which costs travel towards the drop and is why the nod recipes answer a third of the time. 45° of vertical field of view spans every angle in the band at once, so the robot stands still at 260 mm and the answer arrives at 15 Hz. Same 80 held-out staircases:</p> <div class="tw"><table><thead><tr><th>recipe</th><th>success</th><th>answers</th><th>riser error</th> <th>worst margin</th><th>fell or went over</th></tr></thead><tbody> <tr><td>flick, single-shot estimator</td><td class="m">0.362</td><td class="m">77/80</td> <td class="m">220 ± 304 mm</td><td class="m">−65 mm</td><td class="m">15/80</td></tr> <tr><td>creep, wind, look, judge + sonar</td><td class="m">0.300</td><td class="m">27/80</td> <td class="m">8 ± 7 mm</td><td class="m">+75 mm</td><td class="m">0/80</td></tr> <tr><td><b>stand still + VL53L5CX</b></td><td class="m"><b>0.938</b></td><td class="m">80/80</td> <td class="m">13 ± 5 mm</td><td class="m">+185 mm</td><td class="m">0/80</td></tr> </tbody></table></div> <p class="note">That 0.938 is <em>after</em> modelling a zone as the cone it really is — five sub-rays per zone, nearest taken, as the part reports. One ray per zone centre deletes every mixed pixel from a problem that is entirely about a depth discontinuity, and flattered it to 1.000 at 3.8 mm. The flattering number was the model, not the sensor.</p> <h2>Four steps in a row</h2> <p class="sub">{flight_ok} of {len(flights)} flights took all four steps. The cycle is: roll at a measured speed, <b>commit</b> 20 mm before an edge the array has already located, hold attitude through the landing, settle, back off to 75% of the tread — which is both where the array measures best and far enough to approach the next edge deliberately — and repeat.</p> <p class="note"><b>Committing is the whole trick.</b> Reacting cannot work: rolling off a lip at walking pace produces no free fall at all, because the wheel stays on the corner the whole way down, so the accelerometer never sees anything to react to. Meanwhile the velocity loop watches its support vanish and drives the wheels to −4.9 m/s. The robot does not need to detect the edge though — it measured it. Holding attitude across the lip with the speed loop off takes a 100 mm step from 0% to 92%, and a 170 mm step from 0% to 75%.</p> <p class="note"><b>And it stays square.</b> A step taken skewed lands on one wheel, which is the one failure the attitude hold cannot save: at 10° off square the success rate collapses to 10–15% against 65–90% when square. The yaw controller holds the heading the robot approached on, and across four landings the drift stays under <b>0.3°</b>. Worth knowing: the 8 × 8 array <em>cannot</em> measure that skew — at a 280 mm standoff 5° moves the edge distance by about 1 mm, well under the range noise — so squareness has to be held, not sensed.</p> <div class="grid">{"".join(flight_clip(r) for r in flights)}</div> <h2>Going down: {len(down)} attempts at a single step</h2> <p class="sub">{down_ok} landed it. Mapping first, because it decides the shape of any descent: the occlusion condition for the <em>k</em>-th tread reduces to the same D < h × tread / rise with no k in it, so a staircase is self-similar and anything that sees the first tread can geometrically see them all. What limits the map is resolution — 8 rows resolve about <b>2 to 2.5 treads</b>, the second to 25–30 mm. A one-step lookahead, not a flight.</p> <p class="note"><b>And it cannot take the step.</b> Judged on staying under 46°, one step at a time: 25% at a 40 mm lip, 8% at 80 mm, <b>0% from 100 mm up</b>. The enemy is not the drop, it is the robot's own velocity loop: one axle means both wheels leave the ground together, and for ~150 ms the balance law servos against nothing — unloaded wheels run from 0.56 to 5.78 m/s in 50 ms and the reaction throws the body to 90–110°. The accelerometer sees the whole event (|a| falls to ~2 m/s² in free fall, spikes to ~176 on touchdown), so the controller now holds the balance law off while airborne and damps the wheels only. Compare the two 40 mm clips: with the catch the body peaks at 7°, without it at 94°. It is a real fix for a real bug, and it is still not a step primitive. That needs to be trained, the way the stand-up was.</p> <div class="grid">{"".join(down_clip(r) for r in down)}</div> <h2>Why it is this hard</h2> <p class="sub">Where the first tread is visible from, measured kinematically: body pitch in degrees that puts returns on it, against how far back the robot stands. Beyond about 550 mm there is no angle that works — the ray that clears the step nose already overflies the whole first tread.</p> <div class="tw"><table><thead><tr><th>standoff</th><th>80 mm riser</th><th>100 mm riser</th> <th>170 mm riser</th></tr></thead><tbody>{band}</tbody></table></div> <p class="note">At a 170 mm riser that band is one three-degree cell wide per standoff, which is why a fixed recipe scores 0 out of 10 there while managing 0.60 at 130 mm. And the nod is not free: gravity acting over the time the body is tilted adds about 1 m/s of forward speed per 34° of lean, and shedding it costs 0.2–1.1 m of travel towards the drop. Entering the nod <em>reversing</em> is what pays for it; entering it rolling forwards loses the robot outright, which is the clip above.</p> <h2>Three ways the reward was wrong</h2> <p class="sub">Each failure was the optimiser reading my numbers correctly.</p> <div class="why">{why}</div> <p class="note">The rule they share is now an assertion that runs when the environment is imported: the drop has to cost more than the best possible reading is worth, and never looking has to cost more than a safe bad look.</p> <footer>Rendered by <span class="mono">sim/stairs_video.py</span> through the same environment, controller, sensor noise and estimator as <span class="mono">ml/evaluate_stairs.py</span>; this page is generated from the clips' own telemetry by <span class="mono">site/build_stairs.py</span>.</footer> </main></body></html>''') print(f"wrote {OUT} ({OUT.stat().st_size // 1024} kB), {len(rows)} clips, " f"{sum(r['kb'] for r in rows) // 1024} MB of video") if __name__ == "__main__": main()

"""Build the artifact copy of site/index.html: de-skeletoned AND self-contained. Two separate traps live here, and the viewer has been dark because of them. 1. **The double wrap.** The Artifact tool wraps whatever it publishes in its own `<!doctype html><html><head>`, and site/index.html is already a complete document (it has to be, site/ is served directly too). Publishing it raw nests one document inside the other and the importmap ends up inside the body, where it does nothing. So the skeleton tags are stripped. 2. **Module resolution.** Even de-skeletoned, the page imported `three` through an importmap - first from a CDN, then from `./vendor/`. An importmap value resolves against the document's base URL, and an artifact page's base URL is not something this script can know; get it wrong and the import 404s, the module never runs, and the canvas stays blank with nothing in the page to show for it. So the artifact copy has NO imports at all: three.js and OrbitControls are inlined ahead of the viewer code, their export/import statements removed, and `THREE` is rebuilt as a plain object from three's own export list. Nothing left to resolve. The repo's site/index.html keeps the importmap and site/vendor/, which is the right shape for `python3 -m http.server -d site` and for any ordinary web host. python tools/artifact_page.py [out.html] """ import pathlib, re, sys ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] SITE = ROOT / "site" DEFAULT_OUT = pathlib.Path("/private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-tuan-data-projects-2-wheel-balanced-bot/" "b4c1c743-8a14-49ee-8c13-d1a132f33e0f/scratchpad/publish/index.html") def three_bundle(): """three.js + OrbitControls as plain script text, with every import and export removed.""" three = (SITE / "vendor" / "three.module.js").read_text() orbit = (SITE / "vendor" / "addons" / "controls" / "OrbitControls.js").read_text() m = re.search(r"^export \{([^}]*)\};\s*$", three, re.M) if not m: raise SystemExit("three.module.js: no trailing export block - check the version") names = [n.strip() for n in m.group(1).split(",") if n.strip()] if any(" as " in n for n in names): raise SystemExit("three.module.js exports an alias; the THREE object below would be wrong") three = three[:m.start()] + three[m.end():] orbit = re.sub(r"^import \{[^}]*\} from ['\"]three['\"];\s*", "", orbit, flags=re.M | re.S) orbit = re.sub(r"^export \{[^}]*\};\s*$", "", orbit, flags=re.M) if "import" in orbit.split("\n")[0]: raise SystemExit("OrbitControls: import block not removed") # OrbitControls goes in a closure, NOT at the top level beside three.js. Both declare `_ray` # (and others) at module scope, and concatenating them raises "Identifier '_ray' has already # been declared" - which kills the whole module, so the canvas stays blank with no clue why. # node --check caught it; a browser would just have shown nothing, again. return (three + "\nconst THREE = {" + ", ".join(names) + "};\n" + "const OrbitControls = (function(){\n" + orbit + "\nreturn OrbitControls;\n})();\n") def build(src_html=None): s = (src_html or (SITE / "index.html")).read_text() if not isinstance(src_html, str) else src_html # 1) no imports: drop the importmap and the two import lines, inline the libraries instead s = re.sub(r'<script type="importmap">.*?</script>\s*', "", s, flags=re.S) s = re.sub(r"^\s*import \* as THREE from ['\"]three['\"];\s*$", "", s, flags=re.M) s = re.sub(r"^\s*import \{OrbitControls\} from ['\"][^'\"]*OrbitControls\.js['\"];\s*$", "", s, flags=re.M) s = s.replace('<script type="module">', "<script type=\"module\">\n" + three_bundle(), 1) # 2) no nested document: the Artifact tool supplies the skeleton for pat in (r"(?is)<!doctype[^>]*>", r"(?is)</?html[^>]*>", r"(?is)</?head[^>]*>", r"(?is)<body[^>]*>", r"(?is)</body>"): s = re.sub(pat, "", s) return s.strip() + "\n" def main(): out = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else DEFAULT_OUT s = build() out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) out.write_text(s) low = s.lower() bad = [] if low.count("<!doctype") or low.count("<html") or low.count("<head>"): bad.append("skeleton tags survived") if "importmap" in low: bad.append("importmap survived") if re.search(r"^\s*import\s", s, re.M): bad.append("an import statement survived") if "new THREE.WebGLRenderer" not in s or "class OrbitControls" not in s: bad.append("the bundle did not land") print(f"wrote {out} ({len(s)//1024} kB)") print(" checks:", "FAILED - " + "; ".join(bad) if bad else "clean: no skeleton, no imports, " "three and OrbitControls inlined") return 1 if bad else 0 if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main())
